# Deploying the Quarkus SSR demo

Runs the [Pathland Quarkus demo](pathland-quarkus-demo/) (server-side HTML at any
path + live `/ws` deltas) as a container — the application evidence for the Restack
proposal (issue #71, `docs/PREAPPLICATION-TODO.md`).

The image is multi-stage: it builds the Java reactor with the Quarkus
Mandrel 25 builder image, compiles the demo to a **GraalVM native executable**
(no JVM at runtime), and copies only the native binary into the UBI9 Quarkus
micro image. No Rust toolchain or native library is needed.

## Requirements

- Docker with BuildKit (or Podman)
- Roughly **6–8 GB RAM** available to the build (native-image is memory-hungry)
- No local GraalVM/Mandrel installation — the builder image provides it
- **x86_64** target (`linux/amd64`); build with `--platform linux/amd64` when
  building on Apple Silicon
- Quarkus 3.39 requires **GraalVM/Mandrel 25+**; the Dockerfile pins the
  `jdk-25` Mandrel builder image

## Build

From the repository root (build context must be the root — the Java reactor plus
the generated base-design assets under
`lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-html/assets/`):

```bash
docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64 \
  -f lib/java/pathland-quarkus-demo/Dockerfile \
  -t pathland-quarkus-demo .
```

The image's Maven step selects both `pathland-quarkus-demo` and
`pathland-quarkus-deployment`. The deployment module is not a Maven dependency of
the demo, but the runtime extension descriptor validates its dependencies against
it; omitting it makes a fresh (empty `~/.m2`) build fail Quarkus extension
verification.

The Mandrel builder image does not ship Maven, so the build uses the committed
`lib/java/mvnw` wrapper. The first build downloads the Maven distribution and all
dependencies; subsequent builds reuse the BuildKit Maven cache. Native
compilation itself typically takes several minutes.

## Run locally

```bash
docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 pathland-quarkus-demo
# → http://localhost:8080
```

A quick check that it serves:

```bash
curl -I http://localhost:8080/          # 200, text/html
curl http://localhost:8080/ | grep -o 'data-pathland-id'   # hydrated SSR markup
curl -sSI https://<host>/ | grep -i '^strict-transport-security'   # HSTS
```

Also verify the native-specific paths:

```bash
curl -I http://localhost:8080/_pathland/assets/audio/track1.mp3   # Range/seek
curl -I http://localhost:8080/_pathland/sw.js                     # Service-Worker-Allowed
curl -I http://localhost:8080/_pathland/base-<hash>.css           # linked base design
curl -sS http://localhost:8080/q/health
curl -sS http://localhost:8080/q/metrics | head
```

The player at `/` embeds the `/ad` app through a same-server `ProxyView`. The
proxy uses the JDK `java.net.http.WebSocket` client; confirm the sponsored slot is
interactive in the native container. If it is not, add
`--initialize-at-run-time=java.net.http,jdk.internal.net.http` to
`quarkus.native.additional-build-args` or switch the Quarkus starter to a
WebSockets Next client.

HSTS is app-owned (the extension does not default it): the demo sets
`max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains` in its `application.properties`. Because
that file is baked into the native image, changing it requires a rebuild/redeploy
— a plain restart of an existing container will not pick it up.

State defaults to the in-memory store (no Redis needed for the demo). To use
Redis, pass a `REDIS_URL` and the Redis `StateStore` in `pathland-server-core` is
selected at runtime. The demo's in-memory path is unaffected by native-image; if
you use Redis with non-JDK state types, add GraalVM serialization reachability
metadata for those types.

## Push to a registry

```bash
docker tag pathland-quarkus-demo ghcr.io/<org>/pathland-quarkus-demo:latest
docker push ghcr.io/<org>/pathland-quarkus-demo:latest
```

## Deploy to a host

Any platform that runs a Docker container exposing TCP 8080 works:

- **Render / Railway / Fly.io** — point at the image (or use a Dockerfile deploy);
  set the public port to **8080**. The app binds `0.0.0.0` (see
  `application.properties`). Build the image for `linux/amd64`.
- **Hetzner / any VPS** — `docker run -d -p 8080:8080 --name pathland pathland-quarkus-demo`
  (optionally behind Caddy/nginx; forward `GET /` and the WebSocket `Upgrade`).
- **Platform port override** — the app honors `QUARKUS_HTTP_PORT` if a platform
  assigns a different port.

### Requirements

- **WebSocket support**: the demo keeps the first page live via `/ws` (raw-input
  events + `PLPL` deltas). The reverse proxy / load balancer must forward the
  WebSocket `Upgrade` headers; most PaaS do this by default.
- **Health check**: `GET /` returning 200 with HTML is the simplest probe. The
  container has no separate health endpoint.
- **Memory**: the native executable has a much smaller footprint than the former
  JVM image (which was capped at `-Xmx256m`); the demo is small.

parts.text:
Dockerfile syntax okay and images exist. Should we run the full native build? It would verify end-to-end. Given the user's request and the availability, we should attempt. It may take several minutes. We can run with a long timeout (e.g., 30 min = 1800000 ms). The environment may handle. Let's do it, but first consider that the build context is large (lib/java, lib/rust assets, but .dockerignore excludes target). It may copy a lot. Fine.

Potential issue: The builder image runs as `quarkus` user; `COPY --chown=quarkus:quarkus` works. The `mvnw` wrapper downloads Maven 3.9.9. The native build uses `-Dquarkus.native.native-image-xmx=4g`. Docker Desktop default memory maybe 8GB. Let's try.

We should also consider the `-Dmaven.test.skip=true` and `-pl pathland-quarkus-demo,pathland-quarkus-deployment -am`: The new module `pathland-native-core` is in the base modules but not needed for the demo. `-am` will build only dependencies of the selected modules, not the whole reactor. Since `pathland-quarkus-demo` depends on `pathland-quarkus` and `pathland-demo-views-kotlin`, and `pathland-quarkus` depends on view-core/server-core/render-html, it won't build native-core (not a dependency). Good. But the root reactor's `demos` profile is active; `-pl` selects only the listed modules and their dependencies. `pathland-demo-views-kotlin` is a dependency of the demo, so built. `pathland-quarkus-deployment` explicitly selected. Good.
- Does `-am` include `pathland-native-core`? No, not a dependency. Good.

Let's run the build. We'll capture output to a log to avoid huge output. Use `docker buildx build ... 2>&1 | tee /tmp/pathland-native-build.log`? The tool captures output to a file if large. We can run with `--progress=plain` to see steps. We'll use `--progress=plain`. Set timeout 1800000 (30 min). Let's do it.

parts.text:
The cache mount target `/home/quarkus/.m2` is owned by root because the cache mount creates it root-owned; the `quarkus` user can't write. Need to set uid/gid on the cache mount or use a different cache target. BuildKit cache mount supports `uid`/`gid` options:
`--mount=type=cache,target=/home/quarkus/.m2,uid=1001,gid=0`
or use `target=/tmp/m2` and `-Dmaven.repo.local=/tmp/m2`. Simpler: set `uid=1001` in the mount. The quarkus user's UID is 1001? Likely. The builder image user `quarkus` has UID 1001. Let's verify by running `docker run --rm quay.io/quarkus/ubi9-quarkus-mandrel-builder-image:jdk-25 id` quickly.

===================================================================
--- lib/java/pathland-quarkus-demo/src/main/resources/application.properties	
+++ lib/java/pathland-quarkus-demo/src/main/resources/application.properties	
@@ -1,57 +1,67 @@
 quarkus.http.port=8080
 quarkus.http.host=0.0.0.0
 quarkus.log.category."dev.pathland".level=INFO
 
 # --- HSTS (whole-origin, app-owned) --------------------------------------------
 # The extension deliberately does not default HSTS: it pins the entire origin
 # (all paths/ports, and subdomains with includeSubDomains) in the browser. This
 # demo is served only over HTTPS behind Render's TLS terminator, so opt in here.
 # Drop includeSubDomains if any subdomain may remain on plain HTTP; only add
 # preload if the domain is intentionally submitted to the HSTS preload list.
 quarkus.http.header."Strict-Transport-Security".value=max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains
 
 # --- Same-server proxy demo (spec/PROXY.md) ------------------------------------
 # The music player at / embeds the small ad app mounted at /ad (this same server)
 # as a sponsored slot in its Now Playing pane, via a ProxyView. This is the origin
 # app's base URL the player proxies; point it at another host/port to proxy a
 # remote app instead.
 pathland.demo.ad-url=http://localhost:8080/ad
 
 # --- Per-window id on the first request (issue #155) ---------------------------
 # Opt the DOM client into the service worker that attaches the per-window id to
 # top-level navigations, so the SSR renders the right persisted-state scope on the
 # FIRST paint (instead of defaults that the live connection then corrects). The id
 # never appears in the URL. Off by default; the worker is served at /_pathland/sw.js
 # with Service-Worker-Allowed: / (root scope) and no-cache.
 pathland.service-worker=true
 
 # The DOM client bundle ships in the Quarkus extension jar (`META-INF/resources`)
 # and is served by Quarkus's static handler. The demo's media/icons are served
 # from a disk extraction via DemoAssetsRoute, which sends its own caching headers.
 quarkus.http.static-resources.max-age=168h
 
 # Pathland SSR debug comments: when true, every rendered HTML node is prefixed
 # with a comment naming its component type and the modifiers applied, e.g.
 #   <!-- #1 VStack: spacing=4, alignment=Fill -->
 # Debugging aid — opt-in; the live /ws deltas are unaffected.
 # pathland.debug-html=true
 
 # --- Observability (issue #62) -------------------------------------------------
 # Structured (JSON) console logging — the production-shaped reference app default.
 quarkus.log.console.json.enabled=true
 # Metrics: Micrometer counters/timers at pathland.* are exposed at /q/metrics
 # (Prometheus); health at /q/health (smallrye-health). See pathland-server-core.
 #
 # OpenTelemetry spans per frame send / event batch are OPT-IN. The starter wires the
 # tracing decorator automatically when a Tracer is available, so to enable them just
 # add the extension and point it at a collector:
 #   <dependency>io.quarkus:quarkus-opentelemetry</dependency>
 #   quarkus.otel.exporter.otlp.traces.endpoint=http://localhost:4317
 # (the extension is intentionally NOT a dependency here, so local dev is quiet).
 
+# --- Native image (GraalVM/Mandrel) ---------------------------------------------
+# The starter probes Redis at startup via Lettuce. Lettuce keeps a Netty
+# DnsAddressResolverGroup (built from a DnsNameResolverBuilder) in static fields,
+# and Netty marks that builder for run-time initialization. Quarkus initializes
+# application classes at build time, so those resolver objects would land in the
+# image heap and GraalVM rejects them. Keep the three Lettuce holder classes
+# run-time initialized; the demo defaults to the in-memory state store, so Redis
+# remains optional.
+quarkus.native.additional-build-args=--initialize-at-run-time=io.lettuce.core.resource.DefaultClientResources,--initialize-at-run-time=io.lettuce.core.resource.AddressResolverGroupProvider,--initialize-at-run-time=io.lettuce.core.resource.AddressResolverGroupProvider$DefaultDnsAddressResolverGroupWrapper
+
 # --- SEO document head (issue #45) --------------------------------------------
 # Canonical/OG/Twitter/JSON-LD are emitted by default; the app can refine them
 # per route via PathlandApp.pageMetadata(...).
 pathland.seo.site-name=Pathland Music
 pathland.seo.og-type=website
 pathland.seo.structured-data=true

parts.text: continue

We need to continue. The native build failed due to Netty DNS runtime-init conflict. Let's fix. Options:
1. Add `--initialize-at-build-time=io.netty.resolver.dns.DnsNameResolverBuilder` (and maybe DnsAddressResolverGroup) to native args.
2. Better: avoid the Lettuce Redis initialization at build time. But the error is due to Quarkus initializing classes at build time. The class `DnsNameResolverBuilder` is marked runtime-init by Netty metadata, but an object is in the image heap because `DefaultClientResources` static initialization at build time created it. The suggested fix is to initialize `DnsNameResolverBuilder` at build time. Let's try that exact arg.

We should add it to the demo's `application.properties` as `quarkus.native.additional-build-args=--initialize-at-build-time=io.netty.resolver.dns.DnsNameResolverBuilder`. Then rebuild. But there may be more classes. Let's try.

Alternatively, to avoid Redis entirely, we could modify `StateStores.redisOrFallback` to only create the Redis store when `REDIS_URL`/property is set. But the native-image analysis may still include the code path and initialize `DefaultClientResources` at build time. The error is a build-time initialization issue, not runtime. If the code is reachable, Quarkus may still initialize the class at build time. However, if we guard the call behind a config check, the method is still reachable, but the static initialization of `DefaultClientResources` may not be triggered unless the class is initialized. Quarkus initializes all classes at build time by default, so it may still trigger. The recommended arg is simplest.

Let's add the arg. Need to be careful with `application.properties` comma-separated list escaping. Add:
```
# Native-image: Lettuce/Netty DNS resolver ...
quarkus.native.additional-build-args=--initialize-at-build-time=io.netty.resolver.dns.DnsNameResolverBuilder
```
Then rerun Docker build. It will reuse the Maven cache and compile layers; native step re-runs. Let's do it.

+# time, while Netty marks its DNS builder for run-time initialization; GraalVM

+# at build time (the value holds no sensitive state). The demo defaults to the
+# in-memory state store, so Redis is optional.

+

 # per route via PathlandApp.pageMetadata(...).
 pathland.seo.site-name=Pathland Music

parts.text: Now the object comes from `io.lettuce.core.resource.AddressResolverGroupProvider.addressResolverGroup` (line 50), which has a static field `DEFAULT` or similar. So `AddressResolverGroupProvider` is initialized at build time. We need to mark `io.lettuce.core.resource.AddressResolverGroupProvider` for runtime init too. Let's inspect.

`AddressResolverGroupProvider` has a static `ADDRESS_RESOLVER_GROUP` created from `DefaultDnsAddressResolverGroupWrapper.INSTANCE`. Mark `io.lettuce.core.resource.AddressResolverGroupProvider` for runtime init. But there may be more classes with static fields creating DNS objects. Let's mark both:
- `io.lettuce.core.resource.DefaultClientResources`
- `io.lettuce.core.resource.AddressResolverGroupProvider`
Maybe `io.lettuce.core.resource.AddressResolverGroupProvider$DefaultDnsAddressResolverGroupWrapper` too, because its `INSTANCE` static field creates a `DnsAddressResolverGroup`. Let's inspect.

Mark `io.lettuce.core.resource.AddressResolverGroupProvider$DefaultDnsAddressResolverGroupWrapper` for runtime init. If the wrapper is runtime-init, its static `INSTANCE` won't be in the image heap; `AddressResolverGroupProvider` static init at build time calls `DefaultDnsAddressResolverGroupWrapper.INSTANCE`, which would trigger runtime-init class at build time? GraalVM would error "class initialized at build time despite runtime-init". So mark `AddressResolverGroupProvider` runtime-init too. Then its static initializer runs at runtime and creates the wrapper. Good.

Also `DefaultClientResources` static init uses `AddressResolverGroupProvider.addressResolverGroup()`; if `DefaultClientResources` is runtime-init, it calls at runtime. Good.

So add:
`--initialize-at-run-time=io.lettuce.core.resource.DefaultClientResources,io.lettuce.core.resource.AddressResolverGroupProvider,io.lettuce.core.resource.AddressResolverGroupProvider$DefaultDnsAddressResolverGroupWrapper`

But note `quarkus.native.additional-build-args` is a comma-separated list; the `$` is fine. The value contains commas, which is the separator. We want one argument with comma-separated classes after `=`; MicroProfile Config splits on commas at the top level, so `--initialize-at-run-time=a,b,c` would be split into three list elements: `--initialize-at-run-time=a`, `b`, `c` — wrong! The Quarkus property is a list; each element is passed as a separate argument. We have all needed. Need to decide whether to include native-image metadata in the Redis module. Let's verify the exact `native-image.properties` syntax and whether the three flags are sufficient. We can't test without implementing. But we can propose it as a best-effort. Alternatively, we can omit the metadata and document that Redis-in-native requires flags. The user's immediate goal is the demo native build, which won't include Lettuce. For a clean split, the Redis module can own its native metadata. I think including it is good.

But we need to be careful: `native-image.properties` `Args` is read by GraalVM and applied to the image. It will apply to any app that includes the module. The flags:
```
Args = --initialize-at-run-time=io.lettuce.core.resource.DefaultClientResources \
       --initialize-at-run-time=io.lettuce.core.resource.AddressResolverGroupProvider \
       --initialize-at-run-time=io.lettuce.core.resource.AddressResolverGroupProvider$DefaultDnsAddressResolverGroupWrapper
```
The `\` line continuation in properties: Java properties supports backslash continuation. GraalVM reads it as a properties file. Good. However, the `$` in the class name is fine. This should prevent the static holders from being initialized at build time. Whether there are additional Lettuce/Netty DNS holders is unknown. We can note that the metadata is best-effort and that native Redis may need further flags/serialization config. The demo doesn't use it.

Alternative: Instead of moving only Redis, we could make the Redis store not initialize DNS at all by using a simpler `DnsResolver` or `SocketAddressResolver`? Not worth.

Now, module naming: `pathland-state-redis` vs `pathland-server-redis`. The user said "Clean redis module split". The existing package is `dev.pathland.state.redis`; artifact `pathland-state-redis` is natural. Add it to the root modules.

- Move `StateStores.java` to the new module as `dev.pathland.state.redis.RedisStateStores` with method `redisOrFallback`.
- Delete `dev.pathland.server.StateStores`.
- The Quarkus/Spring starters no longer call it. Apps can call `RedisStateStores.redisOrFallback` from their `StateStore` bean.
- Alternatively, keep the class name `StateStores` but in the new package. The docs can say `RedisStateStores`. I'll propose `RedisStateStores` for clarity.

Now, the Quarkus default bean. Need to confirm `@DefaultBean` is appropriate. In Quarkus Arc, `@DefaultBean` on a producer method means it's used only if no other bean of that type exists. If an app defines a `@Produces @Singleton StateStore`, the default is disabled. Good. The `PathlandRegistryProducer.host(PathlandTelemetry telemetry, StateStore store)` will inject the app's or default. Good.
- Could also make the default producer `@Singleton` and `@DefaultBean`. Fine.
- The extension's `PathlandRegistryProducer` is `@ApplicationScoped`; producer methods can be static or instance. Fine.

Spring: `pathlandStateStore()` returns `new InMemoryStateStore()`. The app can override with a `StateStore` bean. Good.
- The Spring starter's status.md line 43 says "default StateStore bean (`@ConditionalOnMissingBean` — Redis-or-in-memory)" — update to "in-memory; add pathland-state-redis for Redis".

```xml
<parent> pathland-parent </parent>

  <dependency>org.slf4j:slf4j-api</dependency>
  <dependency>org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter (test)</dependency>
</dependencies>
```
No Kotlin plugin. Java 17. Add release profile? Parent's maven-javadoc-plugin works for Java. The `release` profile in parent attaches sources/javadoc for all modules. For Java-only module, no special profile needed. Good.
- Add `<module>pathland-state-redis</module>` to root POM base modules. Place after `pathland-server-core`? It depends on view-core; server-core depends on view-core and render-html. Maven sorts. I'd place after `pathland-server-core` to group state store with server. Or after `pathland-view-core` because it only depends on it. Either fine. Let's say after `pathland-server-core`.

  ```java
  public static StateStore redisOrFallback(StateStore fallback) {
  ```

 This document provides essential context for AI agents (or human contributors) working on the **Pathland** protocol. It captures the project's direction, architectural decisions, and implementation details to ensure consistency.

 ## Architecture: Rust Opcode Engine
 
 > The canonical core is a **Rust engine** that emits the application's
 > **declarative view structure** — VStack, HStack, Text, spacing, padding,
 > alignment — as a fixed **16-byte opcode ring buffer** into shared linear
 > memory, consumed by host renderers. View components and modifiers are written
 > in Rust with a SwiftUI-like API, and in Kotlin with the hand-written
 > **`dev.pathland.view.dsl` DSL** (reusable JVM library, Java 17+); both drive the
 > engine through the flat **native C ABI** (`pathland-view-native`) over a
 > zero-copy shared ring on desktop. Java hosts mount Kotlin views through
 > `PathlandApp`.
 
 ### The 16-byte Opcode Engine
 
 - Every opcode is exactly **16 bytes**: `Category (1B) | Command ID (1B) | Flags (2B) | A (4B) | B (4B) | C (4B)`, `#[repr(C, packed)]`, little-endian.
 - A 64-byte cache line holds exactly **4 opcodes** → L1-cache-friendly.
 - Opcodes live in a **ring buffer** in linear memory; the guest writes at `writeCursor`, the host reads from `readCursor`; frame boundaries via a monotonic `frameCount` in the header block.
 - **Both directions are binary**: a second **event ring** (host → guest) carries `EVENT`-category opcodes. The renderer writes raw inputs at `eventWriteCursor`; the guest drains them at `eventReadCursor`. Events are 16-byte opcodes through the engine, never a side-channel callback.
 - **Variable-length data** (strings, token paths) lives in a bump **arena**; opcodes reference entries by offset (`[u32 byteLength][bytes...]`), so every opcode stays 16 bytes. A second host-owned **event arena** mirrors this in the host → guest direction (shared-memory event strings, e.g. `TEXT_CHANGED`); over the network, host → guest strings ride the batch's string section.
 - **Window metadata** (`META::SET_WINDOW_METADATA`, field family `TITLE`/`DESCRIPTION`/`LOCALE`) carries the hosting surface's presentation metadata; renderers map it to their own chrome (browser `<title>`/meta description/`<html lang>`, GTK/Qt window title). It is root-scoped and signal-backed, so a route title is a computed over the router. Web-only artifacts (canonical/robots/sitemap) stay host-owned.
 - Spec: **`spec/OPCODE.md`** (primary) + **`spec/CONFORMANCE.md`** (golden vectors). Companion catalogs: **`spec/PRIMITIVES.md`** (views), **`spec/MODIFIERS.md`** (modifiers/properties), **`spec/EVENTS.md`** (events), **`spec/LAYOUT.md`** (frame & layout allocation contract) — draft IDs are allocated there spec-first.
 
 ### Declarative, not positioned (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The engine describes WHAT the UI is — VStack, HStack, Text, spacing,
 > padding, alignment — never WHERE it is. It does not compute layout and does
 > not emit rects.**
 
 - The engine emits **declarative structure** (`TREE` create/delete/insert/remove/move) + **constraint properties** (`PARAMETER` spacing/padding/alignment/FILL/HUG hints).
 - **Native elements everywhere**: each platform's renderer maps the opcode stream onto that platform's native elements — GTK4 widgets on desktop, DOM elements in the browser, HTML server-side — and those native elements lay themselves out. Never a generic canvas unless a platform has no native equivalent.
 - **Reactive emission**: emission is diff-based. Only the nodes that changed emit opcodes (property diffs via `SET_PROPERTY`/`SET_TEXT`, structural diffs via `TREE` opcodes). An unchanged tree emits **zero** opcodes. Signals in the application mark the tree dirty; the engine reconciles.
 - **Zero dynamic heap allocations** during steady-state emission (proven by test).
 
 ### no_std / wasm32 direction guard (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 `pathland-core` and `pathland-view` must remain `#![no_std]` + `alloc` and
 compile for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`. This is the guarantee that the protocol
 core can still target a browser / embedded / remote projection later (goal #15,
 Quarkus SSR + WebSocket). The desktop path (`pathland-view-native`) is the only
 consumer today, but the core must not become desktop-only. Verify with
 `lib/rust/check-wasm.sh` (i.e. `cargo build -p pathland-core -p pathland-view
 --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`).

 `pathland-core::signal` provides writable signals that live in the engine. A
 node binds its text (`Node::text_binding`), a property
 (`Node::property_bindings`) or a **string property** (`Node::string_bindings`,
 e.g. a media controller's `MEDIA_SOURCE`) to a `SignalId`; during emit the engine
 resolves the binding and records the dependency, and `Engine::set_signal`
 re-emits **only the bound nodes** (`SET_TEXT` / `SET_PROPERTY`) — no full tree
 walk. Signal values
 are one of `F32`/`U32`/`Bool`/`Enum`/`Str` (packed to the wire's `u32` value or
 arena string). Foreign hosts reach signals via the flat C ABI

 `node_bind_property`) and the Kotlin/JVM `Signal` type. Binding then calling `emit`

   drains the event ring itself via `pathland_core_drain_events`. Events are never
   delivered through a side-channel callback — they flow through the opcode engine.

 controllers (`Button::clicked` → pointer up, `EventControllerMotion` →
 pointer move/enter/leave), emitting events through the same `Pump::send_input`
 path.

 line belongs to the embedding host — e.g. the JVM's `-cp`/`-D` flags — and must
 not be parsed as GTK options).

   view** (spec/MEDIA.md): `MediaController` owns the resource + transport as
   signals, a `Video` surface renders it, and **audio has no view** — the app
   binds its own buttons/sliders (`controller.attach()` materializes the
   controller's node once, outside any swapping branch).

   `View body()`; a signal read there subscribes that component, and a later write
   re-renders only that component and diffs its retained subtree. A signal bound
   to a node stays fine-grained and does not re-run the body. Plain
   `if`/`when`/`for` works; `ForEach` is the reactive list component.

   the full modifier vocabulary. Styles are Kotlin values

   kapt.

   Java `PathlandApp` bean returns a Kotlin `View`
   (`return () -> MusicPlayerView.make();`); no Kotlin compiler or authoring DSL is
   needed in the host module. Every reusable Kotlin root exposes a public
   constructor or `@JvmStatic make(...)` factory with Java-friendly types.
 - **Consistency** with `pathland_core::constants` is enforced by the
   emitter/HTML tests (golden byte layout + round-trips).

 ## Project Vision
 
 **Pathland is a cross-platform, cross-language UI protocol** that enables retained-mode UI development with multiple renderer backends. It is **protocol-first**, meaning the protocol specification is the source of truth, not any particular implementation.
 
 **Primary Goal**: Write once, run anywhere - Enable UI code to be written once and deployed across web, mobile, desktop, and embedded platforms through different renderer implementations.
 
 **Status**: The Rust opcode engine (16-byte opcode, ring buffer, arena, diff-based reactive emission) is implemented and tested (`cargo test`). See the Architecture section above.
 
 ---
 
 ## CRITICAL ARCHITECTURAL PRINCIPLES
 
 ### Principle 1: Renderer Statelessness (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The renderer MUST NOT retain application state.**
 
 - Renderers are **pure functions** of the opcode stream: same opcodes → same output
 - A renderer MAY retain its **rendered-output tree** (id → native element + computed layout) for drawing, hit-testing, and event routing — this is a cache of its own output, not state
 - The renderer MUST NOT retain component property values as business state, application control flow, or anything the application can change without emitting an opcode
 - The application owns the canonical retained UI tree
 - The engine emits **deltas only**; the renderer applies them to its native elements
 
 **Violation of this principle is a bug, not a feature.**
 
 ### Principle 2: Command-Based Protocol (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The protocol transmits tree mutations as a stream of commands, NOT as serialized trees.**
 
 - Each frame is a **batch of delta commands** describing changes
 - Only **actual changes** are transmitted (diff-based reactive emission)
 - Protocol acts like a **VM instruction stream** / ABI
 - Deterministic, linear decoding without schema lookup or reflection
 
 ### Principle 3: Binary Protocol (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The protocol MUST be binary.**
 
 - Open-source, cross-platform binary format
 - Fixed **16-byte instructions** in a ring buffer shared with the host via linear memory
 - Custom instruction-based bytecode, not schema-driven serialization
 - **Both directions are binary**: tree mutations (app → renderer) AND raw-input events (renderer → app) share the same instruction format, so the wire is language- and platform-agnostic
 
 ---
 
 ## Protocol Quick Reference
 
 The semantic surface is catalogued in the companion specs: **`spec/PRIMITIVES.md`**
 (primitive views + component IDs), **`spec/MODIFIERS.md`** (core modifiers = the
 `PARAMETER` properties), **`spec/EVENTS.md`** (core events + listener bits),
 **`spec/LAYOUT.md`** (frame & layout allocation contract). The
 tables below are a quick recap of the protocol surface; the companion files
 carry the authoritative ID allocations.
 
 > **Implementation status lives in each project's `status.md`**, not in the
 > specs: `lib/rust/crates/pathland-core/status.md`,
 > `lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-gtk/status.md`,
 > `lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-html/status.md`,
 > `lib/java/pathland-view-core/status.md`, `lib/java/pathland-render-html/status.md`,
 > `lib/java/pathland-server-core/status.md`,
 > `lib/java/pathland-spring-boot-starter/status.md`,
 > `lib/java/pathland-quarkus/status.md`,
 > `lib/java/pathland-demo-views-kotlin/status.md`,
 > `lib/java/pathland-desktop-demo/status.md`,
 > and the other Rust crates' `status.md` files.
 
 ### Opcode Format
 
 Every opcode is exactly 16 bytes:
 
 ```
 [Category: u8][Command: u8][Flags: u16][A: u32][B: u32][C: u32]
 ```
 
 See `spec/OPCODE.md` for the full format, ring buffer, arena, and frame lifecycle.
 
 ### Machine-readable protocol manifest
 
 `spec/protocol.tsv` is the target-neutral ID manifest emitted from
 `pathland_core::constants` by `pathland-protocol-manifest` (`cargo run -p
 pathland-protocol-manifest`). It contains only `kind`, `group`, `name`, and
 `value`; each language binding keeps its own representation and validates or
 reads the manifest. There is no Rust→JVM source generation.
 
 The JVM mirror is hand-written and checked by
 `pathland-view-core/src/test/java/.../ProtocolManifestTest`: every manifest row
 must match a Java constant, no extra public numeric constants may exist, and
 `ValueTypes.forProperty` must match `property_value_type`. CI regenerates the
 manifest from Rust and fails on drift.
 
 Engine behavior beyond individual opcodes is specified in `spec/ENGINE.md` and
 enforced by shared self-contained frame traces under `spec/engine-traces/`.
 `pathland-engine-golden` emits them from the Rust engine and the JVM
 `EngineTraceTest` compares its encoded frames byte-for-byte.
 
 ### Categories
 
 | Category | Value | Direction | Description |
 |----------|-------|-----------|-------------|
 | TREE | 0x01 | Guest → Host | Node create/delete/insert/remove/move |
 | PARAMETER | 0x02 | Guest → Host | Constraint properties (spacing, padding, …), design tokens |
 | EVENT | 0x03 | Host → Guest | Raw inputs: pointer down/move/up, key down/up |
 | META | 0x04 | Both | Reset, environment, window metadata |

 | Group | Component | ID |
 |-------|-----------|----|

 ### Key Property IDs
 
 **Stack**: SPACING=0x0001, ALIGNMENT=0x0002, CONTENT_MARGINS=0x0005  
 **Text**: TEXT=0x000A, TEXT_ALIGNMENT=0x000C, LINE_LIMIT=0x000B, TRUNCATION_MODE=0x000D  
 **Style**: COLOR=0x100A, FONT_SIZE=0x1007, FONT_WEIGHT=0x1008, FONT_FAMILY=0x1009, BACKGROUND_COLOR=0x1001, BORDER_WIDTH=0x1003, BORDER_COLOR=0x1004, BORDER_RADIUS=0x1005, OPACITY=0x100D, VISIBLE=0x100E, Z_INDEX=0x100F, CLIPS_TO_BOUNDS=0x1010, PADDING=0x1011, PADDING_TOP/RIGHT/BOTTOM/LEFT=0x1012-0x1015  
 **Special**: WIDTH=0x100B (use -1=FILL, -2=HUG_CONTENT), HEIGHT=0x100C  
 **Semantic**: ROLE=0x2001, STATE=0x2002, ENABLED=0x2003, SELECTED=0x2004, EVENT_LISTENERS=0x2005 (u32 bitmask — which raw events a node wants reported), VALUE=0x2006, MIN_VALUE=0x2007, MAX_VALUE=0x2008, LABEL=0x200A, PROMPT=0x200B  
 **Binding/action**: ACTION_ID=0x2016, BINDING_ID=0x2017, TOGGLE_STYLE=0x2018 (Switch=0, Checkbox=1, Button=2)  
 **Media** (spec/MEDIA.md): MEDIA_CONTROLLER_ID=0x103A (a `VIDEO`'s controller), MEDIA_SOURCE=0x103B, MEDIA_MUTED=0x103C, MEDIA_LOOP=0x103D, MEDIA_RATE=0x103E; PLAYBACK_STATE=0x1035 / MEDIA_POSITION=0x1036 / MEDIA_VOLUME=0x1037 live on the controller
 
 ### Colors
 
 - Literal colors are **sRGB** with D65 white point, packed as `0xAARRGGBB`
 - A color property may instead carry a `DESIGN_TOKEN` reference to a token path
 - Semantic token resolution and theme adaptation are **renderer-owned**
 
 ### Design Token System
 
 **Core Principle**: Application defines intent, overrides, and the theme.
 Renderer defines visual appearance, behavior, defaults, and interaction states.
 
 - The **application owns the theme**: token overrides (base = **light**, `dark.`-prefixed = **dark**) and token references in style properties. Token refs cover COLOR and non-color values (`Length` for spacing/padding/font size/radius/border/frame; `FontFamily.Token` for STRING) in the Rust and Kotlin DSLs.
 - The **renderer owns** default token values (light + dark, the full Tier-1 catalog), token resolution (including explicit `dark.` = forced dark and parent fallback), effective color-scheme detection, interaction states (hover, pressed, focus, disabled), and theme adaptation
 - `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` identifies tokens by **dot-separated string paths** (e.g. `color.primary`, `space.2`) with the standard value-type encoding — there is no separate numeric tokenId system. A `dark.` prefix selects the dark variant (`dark.color.primary`); a `DESIGN_TOKEN` reference whose path starts with `dark.` forces the dark value in either scheme
 - **Runtime theming**: `META::RESET_THEME` clears every app override; a replacement theme is reset + `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` overrides in one frame. `META::SET_COLOR_SCHEME` forces `platform`/`light`/`dark`. Both are renderer state — no node is re-emitted. Java: `Emitter.replaceTheme`/`setColorScheme` + `PathlandSession.setTheme`/`setColorScheme`; Rust: `Engine::reset_theme`/`set_color_scheme`.
 - An unresolvable token reference leaves the property **unset** (renderer default), never an error or stale value.
 - The protocol MUST NEVER describe hover styles, click styles, visual transitions, conditional styling, or layout tuning for interaction states
 - **Deferred**: applying per-component tokens to native GTK/Qt leaf control chrome; web parent-path fallback.
 
 The HTML renderer's default token values are generated from `design/` (see
 "HTML base design" above). Full details: [Design Token System](./spec/OPCODE.md#design-token-system)
 and the canonical catalog / color-scheme contract in [spec/TOKENS.md](./spec/TOKENS.md).

 ## Implementation Guidelines
 
 ### Adding New Component
 1. Add to `component_type` in `lib/rust/crates/pathland-core/src/constants.rs`
 2. Document in `spec/OPCODE.md`
 3. Implement the component type in `pathland-core` (if it affects the retained tree)
 4. Implement native-element mapping in the target renderer (Goal 3–5)
 5. Update the affected project(s)' `status.md`
 
 ### Adding New Property
 1. Add to the appropriate property module in `constants.rs`
 2. Document in `spec/OPCODE.md`
 3. Handle the value type in `pathland-core`'s diff emission (if a stack/text/size property)
 4. Implement in each renderer's property application
 5. Update the affected project(s)' `status.md`
 
 ### Modifying Protocol
 1. Update `spec/OPCODE.md` first (and `spec/CONFORMANCE.md` vectors)
 2. Update `constants.rs` and `pathland-core` encoding/emitters
 3. Run `cd lib/rust && cargo run -p pathland-protocol-manifest` and commit the
    updated `spec/protocol.tsv`
 4. Update the hand-written JVM protocol constants (the Java manifest test fails
    with the exact missing/stale row otherwise)
 5. If emission behavior changed, run
    `cargo run -p pathland-engine-golden -- --emit` and commit the trace fixtures
 6. Verify backward compatibility; update `pathland-core`/renderers + tests
 7. Update the affected project(s)' `status.md`
 
 ### Changing the Wire Format
 - Bump the wire `version` field in `spec/OPCODE.md` and `pathland-core`'s header (currently 1). Pre-release format changes are acceptable while version stays 1.
 
 ### Keeping implementation status updated (MANDATORY)
 
 **The agent MUST keep the per-project `status.md` files in sync with the code.**
 Whenever you land a protocol or renderer change — a new component/property/
 command/event, a new encoder/decoder, a new widget mapping, a new modifier or
 renderer feature, a test that proves new surface — **update the affected
 project's `status.md`** (Implemented / Not implemented / gaps) in the same
 change. The specs (`spec/`) describe the protocol contract only and MUST NOT
 carry implementation status; status lives in `status.md` next to each
 implementing project.
 
 ---
 
 ## Common Pitfalls
 
 ### NEVER Do These
 | Anti-Pattern | Why Wrong | Correct |
 |--------------|-----------|---------|
 | Renderer stores application state | Violates statelessness | Application owns the tree |
 | Engine computes layout / emits rects | Violates declarative model | Emit structure + constraints; native elements lay out |
 | Send full trees | Inefficient | Diff-based reactive emission |
 | String property names | Larger payloads | Use numeric IDs |
 | String component names | Larger payloads | Use numeric IDs |
 | Generic RGB | Ambiguous | Explicitly sRGB |
 | Hover styles in protocol | Renderer job | Define in theme |
 | Heap allocation in steady-state emission | Slow | Preallocated snapshot slab + arena |

 ## Pathland Mindset
 
 **Always remember**:
 1. Protocol is King
 2. Renderers are Dumb (execute commands only)
 3. Applications are Smart (generate commands)
 4. Only Changes Matter (transmit mutations / reactive emission)
 5. Binary is Beautiful (efficient, deterministic)
 
 **When in doubt**: Check `spec/OPCODE.md`, the conformance vectors in `spec/CONFORMANCE.md`, and the companion catalogs (`spec/PRIMITIVES.md`, `spec/MODIFIERS.md`, `spec/EVENTS.md`, `spec/LAYOUT.md`), and the reference implementation (`pathland-core`). Ask: "Does this maintain stateless renderers?" "Does this only transmit actual changes?" "Does this describe WHAT the UI is, never WHERE?" "Is this representable as a 16-byte opcode in any language?"

 # Deploying the Quarkus SSR demo
 
 Runs the [Pathland Quarkus demo](pathland-quarkus-demo/) (server-side HTML at any
 path + live `/ws` deltas) as a container — the application evidence for the Restack
 proposal (issue #71, `docs/PREAPPLICATION-TODO.md`).
 
 The image is multi-stage: it builds the Java reactor with the Quarkus
 Mandrel 25 builder image, compiles the demo to a **GraalVM native executable**
 (no JVM at runtime), and copies only the native binary into the UBI9 Quarkus
 micro image. No Rust toolchain or native library is needed.
 
 ## Requirements
 
 - Docker with BuildKit (or Podman)
 - Roughly **6–8 GB RAM** available to the build (native-image is memory-hungry)
 - No local GraalVM/Mandrel installation — the builder image provides it
 - **x86_64** target (`linux/amd64`); build with `--platform linux/amd64` when
   building on Apple Silicon
 - Quarkus 3.39 requires **GraalVM/Mandrel 25+**; the Dockerfile pins the
   `jdk-25` Mandrel builder image
 
 ## Build
 
 From the repository root (build context must be the root — the Java reactor plus
 the generated base-design assets under
 `lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-html/assets/`):
 
 ```bash
 docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64 \
   -f lib/java/pathland-quarkus-demo/Dockerfile \
   -t pathland-quarkus-demo .
 ```
 
 The image's Maven step selects both `pathland-quarkus-demo` and
 `pathland-quarkus-deployment`. The deployment module is not a Maven dependency of
 the demo, but the runtime extension descriptor validates its dependencies against
 it; omitting it makes a fresh (empty `~/.m2`) build fail Quarkus extension
 verification.
 
 The Mandrel builder image does not ship Maven, so the build uses the committed
 `lib/java/mvnw` wrapper. The first build downloads the Maven distribution and all
 dependencies; subsequent builds reuse the BuildKit Maven cache. Native
 compilation itself typically takes several minutes.
 
 ## Run locally
 
 ```bash
 docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 pathland-quarkus-demo
 # → http://localhost:8080
 ```
 
 A quick check that it serves:
 
 ```bash
 curl -I http://localhost:8080/          # 200, text/html
 curl http://localhost:8080/ | grep -o 'data-pathland-id'   # hydrated SSR markup
 curl -sSI https://<host>/ | grep -i '^strict-transport-security'   # HSTS
 ```
 
 Also verify the native-specific paths:
 
 ```bash
 curl -I http://localhost:8080/_pathland/assets/audio/track1.mp3   # Range/seek
 curl -I http://localhost:8080/_pathland/sw.js                     # Service-Worker-Allowed
 curl -I http://localhost:8080/_pathland/base-<hash>.css           # linked base design
 curl -sS http://localhost:8080/q/health
 curl -sS http://localhost:8080/q/metrics | head
 ```
 
 The player at `/` embeds the `/ad` app through a same-server `ProxyView`. The

 ## Push to a registry
 
 ```bash
 docker tag pathland-quarkus-demo ghcr.io/<org>/pathland-quarkus-demo:latest
 docker push ghcr.io/<org>/pathland-quarkus-demo:latest
 ```
 
 ## Deploy to a host
 
 Any platform that runs a Docker container exposing TCP 8080 works:
 
 - **Render / Railway / Fly.io** — point at the image (or use a Dockerfile deploy);
   set the public port to **8080**. The app binds `0.0.0.0` (see
   `application.properties`). Build the image for `linux/amd64`.
 - **Hetzner / any VPS** — `docker run -d -p 8080:8080 --name pathland pathland-quarkus-demo`
   (optionally behind Caddy/nginx; forward `GET /` and the WebSocket `Upgrade`).
 - **Platform port override** — the app honors `QUARKUS_HTTP_PORT` if a platform
   assigns a different port.
 
 ### Requirements
 
 - **WebSocket support**: the demo keeps the first page live via `/ws` (raw-input
   events + `PLPL` deltas). The reverse proxy / load balancer must forward the
   WebSocket `Upgrade` headers; most PaaS do this by default.
 - **Health check**: `GET /` returning 200 with HTML is the simplest probe. The
   container has no separate health endpoint.
 - **Memory**: the native executable has a much smaller footprint than the former
   JVM image (which was capped at `-Xmx256m`); the demo is small.

 # pathland-quarkus — implementation status
 
 **Last updated:** November 7, 2026
 
 Quarkus extension for Pathland: SSR at any path, live deltas over each
 app's reserved `/{base}/ws`, per-session state. Adding this extension + a
 `PathlandApp` CDI bean gives a running app; `MountedApp` beans host more apps at
 their own subpaths (the BFF layout). Author the root view with
 `pathland-view-core`'s Kotlin DSL; Java hosts return Kotlin views from a
 `PathlandApp` bean. The extension also provides the `dev.pathland.quarkus.kotlin`
 capability and pulls in `quarkus-kotlin`.
 
 ## Implemented
 
 - **Security defaults (issue #63)**: the deployment module contributes
   overridable runtime defaults via `RunTimeConfigurationDefaultBuildItem`:
   `quarkus.http.cors.enabled=true` (no origins → same-origin, which covers
   WebSocket upgrades because the CORS filter runs before routes),
   `quarkus.websockets-next.server.max-message-size`/`max-frame-size=65536`, and
   CSP + `X-Content-Type-Options`/`Referrer-Policy`/`X-Frame-Options` headers via
   `quarkus.http.header.*`. See `docs/HARDENING.md` for overrides, CSP rollout,
   reverse-proxy/TLS guidance, and edge rate limiting. The `wid` handshake query
   is validated by server-core (`WindowIds`). **HSTS is deliberately not an
   extension default** — it is a whole-origin, persistent browser policy that
   also covers other apps on the same server, so it is owned by the application
   or edge; the Quarkus demo opts in via `application.properties`.
   `docs/HARDENING.md` documents the directives and override guidance.
 - **Hosted deployments work by default**: the same defaults set
   `quarkus.http.proxy.proxy-address-forwarding`, `allow-x-forwarded`, and
   `enable-forwarded-host` to `true`, so a TLS-terminating PaaS (Render, Fly,
   Heroku, Cloud Run) gets a correct same-origin WebSocket check and an external
   SSR canonical URL with zero configuration. These are lowest-priority defaults;
   application config (including
   `quarkus.http.proxy.proxy-address-forwarding=false`) always wins.
 - **Topic hub bean**: the extension produces a `PathlandSignalHub` singleton
   (`host.signalHub()`: root mount, else the first mount) for external UI updates.
   `TopicSubscriptionsTest` mounts a `/topics` app and proves a background-thread
   publish reaches only the session subscribed for that subject.
 - **Java host / Kotlin views**: `CounterApp` is a Java CDI bean whose
   `newRoot()` returns a Kotlin-authored fixture view; the multi-session
   WebSocket tests prove SSR + live deltas work through that mount.
 
 - **Crawler endpoints**: `/robots.txt` (text/plain) and `/sitemap.xml` (application/xml) are real routes before the SPA catch-all, so Lighthouse does not parse the HTML shell as robots.txt.
 - **SEO document head (issue #45)**: `IndexResource` derives the canonical URL
   from `UriInfo` and passes host-default `PageMetadata` to the registry;
   `PathlandApp.pageMetadata(...)` may override it per route before the first
   paint. Canonical/OG/Twitter/JSON-LD are on by default and configurable via
   `pathland.seo.{enabled,site-name,image,og-type,twitter-card,twitter-site,structured-data}`.
 
 - **`PathlandSocket`** — `@WebSocket("/_pathland/ws")` for the root app: 1:1 sessions
   per connection (a fresh `uiId` per connection + the client's `wid` state scope from
   the `?wid=` query param), binary events routed into the root registry of the
   `PathlandHost`. **Stateless (critical)**: quarkus-websockets-next endpoints default
   to `@Singleton` — one shared instance for all connections — so the per-connection
   ids come from `connection.id()` + the handshake and the `QuarkusConnection` adapters
   live in a map keyed by connection id. Memoizing `uiId`/`wid`/`transport` on the
   shared instance collapsed every connection onto ONE session (multiple browsers shared
   one UI model — a probe or second tab drove the first tab's session).
 - **`MountedPathlandSocket`** — `@WebSocket("/{app}/_pathland/ws")` for mounted apps:
   the `{app}` path param resolves the app's registry. Mount paths are single-segment.
   Same stateless rule as the root socket.
 - **`IndexResource`** — JAX-RS SSR catch-all (`/` + deep links; `/_pathland/**` and the
   Quarkus non-application root `/q/**` — health/metrics — excluded via negative lookahead)
   dispatching to the longest-mount app (prefix stripped);
   SSR renders defaults (no session cookie — per-window state arrives over the WS);
   per-app framework files (`/{app}/_pathland/...`, e.g. the mounted app's bundle) are
   served from the shared `/_pathland/**` classpath mount. Quarkus serves the global
   `/_pathland/**` bundle + asset mount from `META-INF/resources` before JAX-RS.
   **The extension jar ships the DOM client bundle** (`META-INF/resources/_pathland/
   dom-renderer-<hash>.js` + the `dom-renderer.current` pointer + the service worker), so
   a consuming application adds the extension and needs no static resources of its own;
   the mounted-base `frameworkFile` path resolves the app's classpath copy first (TCCL),
   then the extension jar, and adds `immutable` caching for the content-hashed bundle. A
   `/_pathland/{file}` JAX-RS route is a fallback for deployments where Quarkus's static
   handler is unavailable (it normally wins).
   **`/_pathland/{name}.css`** (global JAX-RS route + the mounted-base
   `frameworkFile` path) serves the renderer-owned content-hashed base design
   (`HtmlRenderer.baseCss()` at `baseCssName()`) as `text/css` with
   `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`. **`/_pathland/icons/{name}.svg`**
   serves the renderer-owned icon glyphs from the shared Rust renderer
   (`HtmlRenderer.iconSvg` → `pathland_html_icon_svg`) with an `immutable` cache
   header — no static CSS/icon files on any host. SSR links the CSS via
   `PathlandSession` → `renderLinked`.
 - **`PathlandRegistryProducer`** — CDI `@Produces @Singleton` `PathlandHost` from every
   `MountedApp` bean plus the lone `PathlandApp` bean (mounted at `/`); `@Disposes` shuts
   it down. Reads the `pathland.debug-html` config property (default `false`) to enable
   per-node HTML comments in SSR output, and `pathland.service-worker` (default `false`)
   to opt the DOM client into the per-window-id service worker (issue #155) — served at
   `{base}/sw.js` with `Service-Worker-Allowed: /` + `Cache-Control: no-cache`.
 - **`ServiceWorkerFilter`** — serves `/_pathland/sw.js` (root and mounted bases) with
   `Service-Worker-Allowed: /` + `Cache-Control: no-cache`, so the client's root-scoped
   registration succeeds. A `Filters` handler always runs before routes, so it wins over
   Quarkus's static-resource handler (which sends neither header, and whose configured
   max-age would otherwise cache the script and delay update detection). The script is
   resolved through the thread-context classloader first, then the extension's own
   loader, then the system loader: extension runtime classes live in Quarkus's base
   runtime classloader and cannot see the application's `META-INF/resources` copy. The
   extension jar bundles the worker as a fallback (the TS copy script writes it), and
   `pathland-quarkus-demo`'s integration test asserts the headers on both the root and a
   mounted base — the packaged-app classloader path the module-local test could not see.
 - **Observability (issue #62)** — `quarkus-micrometer` (a `MeterRegistry` bean) +
   `quarkus-smallrye-health`: the producer builds a `MicrometerTelemetry` over the
   registry and decorates it with `TracingTelemetry` when a `Tracer` bean is present and
   `quarkus.otel.enabled` (default `true`; the extension never touches the OTel API when
   the extension is absent/disabled). `PathlandHealthCheck` (`@Readiness`) reports the
   host UP with `activeSessions`/`mounts` at `/q/health`; the `pathland.*` meters appear
   at `/q/metrics`.
 - **`QuarkusConnection`** — adapts `WebSocketConnection` to `PathlandConnection`.
   Sends are **serialized** (one `sendBinary` subscription in flight, the rest queued),
   and a **send failure closes the connection** so the session drops it and the DOM
   client reconnects + `META::RESYNC` (recoverable) instead of silently stalling on an
   "open" socket that never delivers (the remote seekbar symptom). **Send timeout**: a
   `sendBinary` that neither completes nor fails within 10 s (a half-dead connection /
   a dropped proxy upstream leg) is marked failed and closed — a hung send would
   otherwise wedge the serialized drain forever. **Keep-alive pings**: the connection
   sends a WS-protocol ping every 15 s (browsers auto-pong) to keep the connection warm
   through middleboxes and detect a dead client; `close()` stops the keep-alive
   scheduler (the sockets' `@OnClose` calls it).
 - **Heartbeat** — both sockets reply to a client `META::PING` with a `META::PONG`
   **at the transport layer** (through their `QuarkusConnection`, no actor/session
   dependency, and a PING never creates or wakes a session); spec/OPCODE.md
   §Transport heartbeat.
 - **Failure handling** — `fail()` logs the reason; `close()` (socket `@OnClose`)
   no longer calls `close()` on the already-closed connection (no spurious
   "Connection already closed" noise). A **transient write failure on a connection
   that still reports open is logged, not closed** — only a confirmed-dead channel
   (or a send hung past the timeout) warrants closing. The send-timeout task is
   **cancelled when the send completes**, so a completed-but-late callback can't
   false-time-out and kill a healthy connection. Keep-alive pings are sent directly
   (Vert.x serializes writes — no sync with `sendBinary` needed).
 - `META-INF/beans.xml` so Quarkus discovers the extension.
 - **Native image support** — the deployment module registers the renderer-owned
   `dev/pathland/render/html/base.css` + `.name` resources via
   `NativeImageResourceBuildItem`, so `HtmlRenderer.baseCss()` works in a GraalVM
   native executable without app-level `quarkus.native.resources.includes`.
   JNA is not on the server classpath (the ring interop lives in
-  `pathland-native-core`), so native-image builds do not need JNA substitutions.
+  `pathland-native-core`), and Redis/Lettuce is opt-in via
+  `pathland-state-redis`, so the demo's native image carries neither.
   The demo's Dockerfile builds with the Mandrel 25 builder image and runs the
   resulting executable on the UBI9 Quarkus micro image.
 - **Quarkus extension metadata** — runtime + `pathland-quarkus-deployment`; the
   runtime provides the `dev.pathland.quarkus` capability. The runtime has no
   dependency on the authoring DSL. Tests use Kotlin-authored fixture views to prove
   a Java CDI bean can mount them.
 
 ## App DX
 
 ```java
 @ApplicationScoped
 public class MyApp {
     @Produces @Singleton PathlandApp main() { return () -> new MyHomeView(); }
     @Produces @Singleton MountedApp support() { return MountedApp.of("/support", ...); }
 }
 ```
 
 ## Verified by
 
 Manual: the `pathland-quarkus-demo` renders `/` (the music player, whose Now
 Playing pane embeds the small `/ad` app via a **same-server `ProxyView`**,
 spec/PROXY.md) and `/ad` (the ad app); a WebSocket handshake to `/_pathland/ws`

 covered by `pathland-server-core` tests. `MultiSessionWebSocketTest` (`@QuarkusTest`) opens **100 concurrent real WS
 sessions** against `/_pathland/ws` (via the shared `pathland-server-core` test-jar
 probe) and asserts each connects, re-syncs, gets transport-level PONGs, stays isolated,
 and is never closed by the peer.
 `PathlandObservabilityTest` (`@QuarkusTest`) asserts `/q/health` reports the Pathland
 check UP and `/q/metrics` exposes the `pathland.*` namespace. `BaseCssTest`
 (`@QuarkusTest`) asserts the linked SSR `<link>`, the immutable `text/css`
 response at the global and mounted bases, and a 404 for an unknown hash.

Existing overloads keep the legacy head. - **`PathlandApp`** — the app's root-view factory (`View newRoot()` + optional `theme()`); the single app-specific piece a starter needs. - **`MountedApp`** — `record MountedApp(String path, PathlandApp app)`: one app mounted at a subpath prefix (normalized; `/` = root). Hosts any number of them. - **`PathlandHost`** — the multi-app dispatcher: one `PathlandRegistry` per mounted app (own actor thread, own sessions). `match(requestUri)` resolves the owning registry by **longest mount-prefix match** and reports the **mount-stripped route** (a root mount claims every unclaimed path). Duplicate mount paths are rejected at construction. - **`PathlandRegistry`** — session lifecycle per app: single actor thread, 1:1 sessions keyed by a **per-connection `uiId`** (a fresh id per WebSocket connection, so two windows of the same browser never share a UI model), lazy creation on first environment message, pending connections (each carrying the mount-prefixed state scope from the client's per-window `wid`), `open(uiId, wid, conn)`/`environment`/`dispatch`/`resync`/`close`/`renderHtml`/`shutdown`. New: - `mountPath()`/`base()` — each app's framework base is `//_pathland` (`/_pathland` for the root), emitted as `data-pathland-base` in SSR; - `stateScope(windowId)` — app-qualified state-store scope (`mount:wid`) so apps and windows sharing a store never collide; - `stripRoute(route)` — strips the mount prefix from SSR routes, WS environment ROUTE fields, **and inbound `NAVIGATE` URLs** (browser back/forward sends the real address, e.g. `http://host/app2/home`), so a mounted app always sees its own route space (`/app2/home` → `/home`). `Router.pathOf` is reused for URL→path extraction. - `shutdown()` — serialized on the actor and idempotent: work enqueued after shutdown starts is dropped, sessions are closed on the actor thread, then the executor is stopped and awaited. Teardown can no longer race a queued mount/resync mutating the same emitter (regression-tested by `shutdownSerializesWithQueuedActorWork`). - **Topic subscriptions / external UI updates**: `PathlandSignalHub` (one per mount) routes `publish(topic, subject, value)` only to sessions subscribed to that exact `(topic, subject)` pair (global topics use the reserved `GlobalSubject` singleton and the two-argument `publish(topic, value)` overload; still only subscribed sessions update); `SessionSubscriptions` holds each session's local mirror, coalesces publishes latest-wins, schedules one actor drain, and unregisters on close/unsubscribe. `PathlandSession.submit(Runnable)` hands arbitrary work to the session actor from any thread; a session context is installed around every actor task (mount, dispatch, drain, theming) so `topic(...)` resolves during render. `PathlandHost.signalHub()`/`signalHub(mount)` expose the hub. Telemetry: `topics.published`/`coalesced`/`dropped`. See `docs/external-updates.md` and `TopicsTest`. - **Per-window isolation (no session cookie)**: session identity (the `uiId` map key) is deliberately separate from the persisted-state scope (the client's `wid`, carried only on the WebSocket URL — never in the page URL, so the address bar stays clean). The SSR request therefore has no `wid`: `renderHtml(route, wid)` with a null `wid` renders defaults; the client's live session is scoped by the WS `wid`, and a same-tab reload re-syncs that window's persisted state over the WebSocket. The old `session` cookie is removed. - **`PathlandSession`** — per-session: builds the `Platform.ACTIVE_PATH` signal, mounts `app.newRoot().modifiers(environmentBinding(e -> e.key(ACTIVE_PATH).value(activePath)))`, **delta-batched send-on-`endFrame`** (`DeltaBatcher` coalesces per-signal frames into one batch — flush ~20 ms or 16 KB, string offsets rebased — so a continuous input burst can't overflow a remote WebSocket send queue), `applyEnvironment` (re-route guard-aware via the bound router), `dispatch` (tap/nav-intent/text/value/date/NAVIGATE), `resync`, `renderHtml`, `close`. Runtime theming: `setTheme(ThemeData)`, `resetTheme()`, and `setColorScheme(ThemeMode)` emit one `META::RESET_THEME` + `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` frame or `META::SET_COLOR_SCHEME` to the live client (renderer state; no tree re-emission). The SSR document keeps the mount theme until a resync/reload. `sendBatch` drops the connection on any send failure (a client reconnect then re-syncs via `META::RESYNC` instead of silently stalling on an "open" socket); `closeConnection` best-effort closes an `AutoCloseable` adapter (the starters now close their underlying WebSocket on failure). Now takes the app's `base` and `stateScope` explicitly (the registry supplies them). - **`DeltaBatcher`** — merges session delta frames (opcodes + a single rebased string section) and flushes as one network batch on a timer/byte threshold; the Java analogue of the Rust transport's `Batcher`. It owns the per-session **message sequence** (stamped on each flushed batch via `FrameCodec.encodeFrame(frame, sequence)`) so the DOM client can detect a lost batch and recover with `META::RESYNC` (spec/OPCODE.md §Sequence gap detection); an empty flush consumes no sequence. The **sender runs OUTSIDE the monitor** — a blocking/queueing send can never stall the actor thread's `append` or the flush scheduler. Coalescing tests cover merging + rebasing, a 100-frame burst collapsing to one send, incrementing sequences, and a blocking sender not holding the lock. - **`PathlandConnection`** — the transport seam (`send(byte[])`/`isOpen()`); each starter adapts its WebSocket type to it. - **Observability seam** — `PathlandTelemetry` (default `NOOP`): the runtime emits session open/close, inbound event batches, inbound drops (oversize/rate), flushed batches (frames/opcodes/bytes + merge-encode time), SSR render latency, resync requests, and send failures; the host binds a pull-based active-sessions gauge. `PathlandHost`/`PathlandRegistry`/ `PathlandSession`/`DeltaBatcher` thread it through (a host with no telemetry pays nothing). This module also ships the `dev.pathland.observability` Micrometer + OpenTelemetry adapters; the starters auto-wire them. Logging is **SLF4J** (both frameworks bind it) — the old ad-hoc `System.out` is gone. See issue #62. - **Concurrency stress** — `RegistryConcurrencyTest`: 100 sessions driven through the registry concurrently (clicks on each session's button) while SSR-style requests construct throwaway sessions on request threads — the shared-actor / global-`Scheduler` cross-session corruption guard. Each session must reach exactly its own click count (no lost effects, no cross-session values). - **Shared WS test harness** — `dev.pathland.server.test.{WsSession,MultiSessionProbe}` (a JDK-WebSocket client speaking the PLPL protocol: env/resync/click/ping) lives in this module in main scope, so package builds resolve it as a normal jar; the starters' 100-session stress tests reuse it. -- **`StateStores`** — default state store: Redis when reachable, else the supplied - fallback. The `dev.pathland.state.redis.RedisStateStore` (Lettuce) ships in this - module too. +- **State stores** — the starters default to `InMemoryStateStore` (or an + app-provided `StateStore` bean). Redis is opt-in via the separate + `pathland-state-redis` module (`RedisStateStores.redisOrFallback`), so server + runtimes and native-image builds that use in-memory state never carry Lettuce. - **Observability adapters** — `dev.pathland.observability.MicrometerTelemetry` turns the seam into `pathland.*` meters (counters, timers, a distribution summary, a pull-based sessions gauge, every meter tagged by `mount`); the optional `TracingTelemetry` decorator emits an OpenTelemetry span per frame send / inbound event batch / SSR render. Micrometer is a compile dependency; the OTel API is `optional`, so a host that does not enable tracing pays nothing. - **SSR debug comments (property-gated)**: `PathlandSession`/`PathlandRegistry` take a `debugHtml` flag (constructor + `isDebugHtml()`); when set, `renderHtml` uses the renderer's debug mode so every rendered node is prefixed with an HTML comment naming its component and the modifiers applied. The Spring/Quarkus starters bind it to the `pathland.debug-html` property (default `false`). - **Reserved framework root**: `PathlandSession.PATHLAND_BASE` (`/_pathland`) — the SSR page carries the app's base as `data-pathland-base` and the DOM-client bundle is injected at `{base}/dom-renderer-.js` (`PathlandAssets` reads the current name from the `_pathland/dom-renderer.current` manifest on the classpath — shipped in the Spring Boot starter (`static/_pathland/`) and the Quarkus extension (`META-INF/resources/_pathland/`) — resolving through the thread context classloader first so an application-supplied override wins; it falls back to the literal `dom-renderer.js` only when absent) so the client's WebSocket and asset refs resolve from the same reserved prefix (spec DSL.md). The content-hashed name busts the immutable asset cache with a fresh URL per build. The built-in base design is linked the same way: `renderHtml` renders through `HtmlRenderer.renderLinked(frame, root, base)`, so the CSS href is `{base}/base-.css` (token overrides/fit rules stay inline). Multi-app hosts give each mount its own base. - **Per-window-id service worker (opt-in, issue #155)**: `PathlandHost` carries a host-level `serviceWorker` flag (default `false`; one registration covers the whole origin) threaded to every `PathlandRegistry`; `PathlandSession.renderHtml` emits `data-pathland-service-worker="true"` on `` when set, and the DOM client registers `{base}/sw.js` (root scope) / unregisters when absent (the kill switch). `PathlandRegistry.serviceWorkerUrl()` names the served script. `renderHtml` also emits `data-pathland-ssr-scoped="true"` when the request carried a real per-window id, so the client can skip its initial `META::RESYNC` (the SSR was already rendered with that window's state and the live session shares it). ## Not implemented / gaps - No multi-node/shared sessions (each server owns its sessions in-memory). - Topic fan-out is node-local: `PathlandSignalHub` routes to this process's sessions only. A Redis/pub-sub-backed hub (each node fanning out to its local sessions) is a follow-up; the topic name + subject are the stable wire keys. - Quarkus mounted-app WebSocket endpoints require a **single-segment** mount path (the `/{app}` path param); Spring supports any depth. ## Proxy views (spec/PROXY.md) — M1 (live) - **`proxy.ProxyIdMap`** — node-id namespacing: the reserved high range `[0x4000_0000, 0x8000_0000)`, 1024 blocks of `2^20`, the block math, and the opcode remap in both directions (`TREE` node ids + the node-id-bearing `PARAMETER` ops `SET_TEXT`/`SET_PROPERTY`/`SET_DATE` on ingress; `EVENT` targets on egress; `META` untouched). `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` is **not** remapped — its `A` is a token-path arena offset, not a node id (remapping it produced a huge out-of-bounds string offset → the client's RESYNC loop; regression-tested). Pure + unit-tested. - **`proxy.ProxyTransport`** + **`proxy.JdkWebSocketTransport`** — the outbound connection seam (default: the JDK `HttpClient` WebSocket client, no new dependency) with a `Factory` so a starter can swap a native client. - **`proxy.ProxySession`** — one origin connection: sends `META::ENVIRONMENT` + `META::RESYNC`, **remaps** the origin snapshot into the proxy's block and attaches the origin root under the proxy node, forwards live deltas remapped, routes client events back (target unmapped), replies `PONG` to origin `PING`, translates origin `META::RESET` into a **scoped** subtree teardown (never a global reset), tears the subtree down on disconnect (the origin session is per-connection), and reconnects with exponential backoff. While an SSR snapshot is pending, `awaitSnapshot` retries `META::RESYNC` every 500 ms, so a lost first handshake cannot consume the whole SSR budget. The service credential + a cycle-guard instance id ride the handshake headers. **Backpressure** (spec/PROXY.md §8): a "chatty origin" breaker (a per-second batch cap → drop + `RESYNC`) and event coalescing (pointer-moves coalesce by target; discrete events flush immediately). - **`proxy.ProxyHost`** — one `ProxySession` per `PROXY_VIEW` node, each with its own block; routes inbound events whose target is in a proxy range to the owning origin connection; owns the proxy scheduler. `reconcile(wanted)` starts a session for every `PROXY_VIEW` node and closes the session of every node that left the tree; released id blocks go to a **free-block pool** and are reused, so repeated removal/re-add cycles never exhaust the 1024-block range. - **`PathlandSession`** integration — captures `RenderResult.proxyViews()` and registers the emitter's structural-reconcile callback (`Emitter.onStructureReconciled`) to `reconcileProxies()`, so a proxy lives **exactly while its node is in the retained tree** (spec/PROXY.md §7): a `SizeThatFits` slot dropping the candidate that held it closes the origin connection, and re-adding it opens a fresh one (re-seeded by `META::RESYNC`). The host's frames feed the session's `DeltaBatcher` (a single unified sequence); `dispatch` splits proxy-range events to the origin and everything else to the app's own bindings; `close` tears the proxies down. `proxyTransportFactory(...)` lets a host supply a framework transport. - **`PathlandTelemetry`** — `proxyConnected`/`proxyDisconnected`/`proxyBatchDropped`/ `proxyResyncRequested` (all default no-ops). **SSR embed (M2).** `renderHtml` starts the proxies and **blocks** for each origin's snapshot (`ProxySession.awaitSnapshot`, bounded by a 2s timeout), then splices the remapped origin frames into the session's mount frame (`FrameMerger`, reusing the batcher's string rebasing via `FrameRebase`) so the renderer emits **one** document — the origin subtree plus its fit band rules in the same head. The origin's **global** token overrides (`SET_DESIGN_TOKEN`) are **dropped** (live + SSR): a proxied app renders under the **host's** theme, while its token *references* resolve against that theme (spec/PROXY.md §9). A proxy whose origin does not answer in time renders empty (a placeholder) and hydrates over the live connection. A client `META::RESYNC` also replays A's tree **and** asks every origin for a fresh snapshot (`ProxyHost.resyncAll`). **Gaps (M3):** nested proxies and per-proxy theme scoping are deferred (the origin's global overrides are dropped, not scoped, spec/PROXY.md §9). A tiny orphan window remains on removal: an origin batch already queued in the `DeltaBatcher` (≤20 ms) when the proxy node is removed can still create an unattached element in the client's `byId` (not in the DOM); eliminating it needs the `ProxySession` to track the ids it emitted and `DELETE` them on close. ## Verified by `mvn test` — `PathlandSessionTest`: mounts + routes taps through the binding maps, `applyEnvironment`/`resync`/`close` idempotent, registry SSR + lifecycle/teardown, **two windows with the same `wid` still get separate sessions** (a tap to one never reaches the other), and **message-before-open ordering** (environment/resync that race `open` still attach the connection and emit the snapshot). `TopicsTest`: strongly typed `(topic, subject)` routing (customer 43 never sees customer 42's update), every session for a subject updates, global topics reach only subscribed sessions and stay isolated from a same-named scoped topic, rapid publishes coalesce latest-wins, updates run on the session actor, close removes subscriptions, unsubscribe keeps the last value, and a topic outside a session fails on read. `PathlandHostTest`: longest-prefix dispatch + route stripping, mount-boundary respect, no-root-mount 404, per-app base + state scope, duplicate-mount rejection, normalization, SSR emits the mounted app's base. `PathlandTelemetryTest`: a recording telemetry double asserts the registry emits session/event/resync/flush/SSR/close events, the host binds the active-sessions gauge, a failed send reports `connectionFailed`, and `DeltaBatcher` reports the flushed batch. `proxy.ProxyIdMapTest`: the reserved range, block round-trips, overflow rejection, and the opcode remap (TREE/PARAMETER node ids remapped, APPEND/META untouched, EVENT targets unmapped). `proxy.ProxySessionTest` (a fake origin transport): the ENVIRONMENT+RESYNC handshake + handshake headers, snapshot retry when the first RESYNC is lost, snapshot remap + root attachment, delta remap with the string section passed through verbatim, event egress unmapped, pointer-move coalescing, `META::RESET` → scoped teardown, disconnect teardown, and the chatty-origin drop+resync breaker. `proxy.ProxyIntegrationTest`: a `ProxyView` in the app tree opens an origin connection on `connect`, the remapped origin snapshot reaches the client (with the root attached), a client event in the proxy range routes back to the origin unmapped, and the SSR document embeds the origin subtree (remapped ids) in one render. `FrameMergerTest`: splicing a proxy's origin frame into an SSR frame rebases its string offsets (SET_TEXT / LIST / STRING operands) and returns the base unchanged when there is nothing to append. \ No newline at end of file
