@@ -1,121 +1,122 @@
 # pathland-spring-boot-starter — implementation status
 
 **Last updated:** November 7, 2026
 
 Spring Boot auto-configuration for Pathland: SSR at any path, live deltas over each
 app's reserved `/{base}/ws`, per-session state. Adding the starter dependency + a
 `PathlandApp` bean gives a running app; `MountedApp` beans host more apps at their own
 subpaths (the BFF layout).
 
 ## Implemented
 
 - **Security hardening (issue #63)**: the WebSocket handlers no longer hardcode
   `setAllowedOrigins("*")`. The default is Spring's same-origin handshake check
   (the WebSocket CSRF control); cross-origin hosts must be listed explicitly in
   `pathland.allowed-origins` (comma-separated). The handshake `wid` is validated
   by server-core (`WindowIds`). SSR inherits SRI (`integrity="sha384-…"`) from
   `PathlandSession`. CSP/security headers and transport limits are documented in
   `docs/HARDENING.md` (Quarkus supplies secure defaults; Spring apps add them
   through Spring Security/server configuration).
 - **Hosted deployments work by default (issue #45 follow-up)**: a
   lowest-precedence `EnvironmentPostProcessor` contributes
   `server.forward-headers-strategy=framework`, so a TLS-terminating PaaS gets a
   correct WebSocket same-origin check and external SSR canonical URL with zero
   configuration. An explicit `server.forward-headers-strategy` in application
   config always wins (`ForwardedHeaderOverrideTest` pins this).
 - **Topic hub bean**: `PathlandAutoConfiguration` produces a `PathlandSignalHub`
   bean (`host.signalHub()`: root mount, else the first mount) for external UI
   updates. `TopicSubscriptionsTest` mounts a `/topics` app and proves a
   background-thread publish reaches only the session subscribed for that subject.
 - **Java host / Kotlin views**: `KotlinViewMountTest` proves a Java-only
   `@SpringBootApplication` bean returning `PathlandApp` mounts a Kotlin-authored
   fixture view, renders it through SSR, and receives a live signal delta.
 
 - **Crawler endpoints**: `/robots.txt` (text/plain) and `/sitemap.xml` (application/xml) are real routes before the SPA catch-all, so Lighthouse does not parse the HTML shell as robots.txt.
 - **SEO document head (issue #45)**: the SSR controller derives the canonical
   URL from the request and passes host-default `PageMetadata` to the registry;
   `PathlandApp.pageMetadata(...)` may override it per route before the first
   paint. Canonical/OG/Twitter/JSON-LD are on by default and configurable via
   `pathland.seo.{enabled,site-name,image,og-type,twitter-card,twitter-site,structured-data}`.
 
 - **`PathlandAutoConfiguration`** (`@AutoConfiguration`, `@EnableWebSocket` since Spring
   Boot 3.5 no longer auto-enables it) + `META-INF/spring/…/AutoConfiguration.imports`:
-  - default `StateStore` bean (`@ConditionalOnMissingBean` — Redis-or-in-memory),
+  - default `StateStore` bean (`@ConditionalOnMissingBean`, in-memory; add the
+    opt-in `pathland-state-redis` module + a `StateStore` bean for Redis),
   - `PathlandHost` bean (shut down with the context): every `MountedApp` bean plus the
     lone `PathlandApp` bean mounted at `/` (unless an explicit `MountedApp` claims the
     root). Without any app the host is empty and the starter is inert.
   - a `WebSocketConfigurer` registering **one handler per app** at its framework base
     (`/_pathland/ws` for the root, `/{mount}/_pathland/ws` otherwise). Each connection
     gets a fresh `uiId` (its UI model) + the client's `wid` (per-window state scope)
     from the WS `?wid=` query param (kept in `sessionStorage`, never in the page URL),
   - `PathlandIndexController` (SSR catch-all dispatching to the longest-mount app with
     the prefix stripped + a framework static controller serving the bundle + asset mount
     from `classpath:/static/_pathland/**` at both `/_pathland/**` and `/{app}/_pathland/**`;
     the more-specific mapping beats `/{*path}`, and the `!Upgrade` header excludes WS).
     **The starter jar ships the DOM client bundle** (`static/_pathland/dom-renderer-<hash>.js`
     + the `dom-renderer.current` pointer + the service worker), so a consuming application
     adds the dependency and needs no static resources of its own; an app-supplied
     `static/_pathland` copy still wins by classpath order.
     When no static file matches, the controller serves renderer-owned assets from the
     shared Rust renderer: the content-hashed base stylesheet
     (`HtmlRenderer.baseCss()` at `baseCssName()`) as `text/css` with
     `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`, and
     `/_pathland/icons/{name}.svg` glyphs (`HtmlRenderer.iconSvg` →
     `pathland_html_icon_svg`) with an `immutable` cache header — no static CSS/icon
     files on any host, and a host can still override either with a file. SSR links
     the CSS via `PathlandSession` → `renderLinked`.
     The framework controller honors byte-range requests (`206 Partial Content` +
     `Content-Range`, `416` for unsatisfiable ranges, `Accept-Ranges` on the full
     response) — a `<video>` (a `MediaController`'s playback) seeking beyond its
     buffer issues a `Range`
     request, and answering it with a full `200` would make browsers restart the media
     at byte 0.
     SSR renders defaults (no session cookie — per-window state arrives over the WS).
 - **SSR debug comments**: the host reads the `pathland.debug-html` property
   (`@Value("${pathland.debug-html:false}")`) and forwards it to each registry, enabling
   per-node HTML comments in SSR output when set.
 - **Per-window-id service worker (opt-in, issue #155)**: `pathland.service-worker`
   (default `false`) forwards to the host; the SSR emits `data-pathland-service-worker`
   and the controller serves `{base}/sw.js` with `Service-Worker-Allowed: /` +
   `Cache-Control: no-cache` (a stable, uncached script the browser byte-compares).
 - **`SpringConnection`** — adapts `WebSocketSession` to `PathlandConnection`.
   `AutoCloseable`: a failed send surfaces as a close (the session's
   `closeConnection` closes the underlying session) so the DOM client reconnects +
   `META::RESYNC` instead of silently stalling on an open socket.
 - **Heartbeat** — the socket replies to a client `META::PING` with a `META::PONG`
   **at the transport layer** (through its `SpringConnection`, no actor/session
   dependency; spec/OPCODE.md §Transport heartbeat).
 - **Observability (issue #62)** — `spring-boot-starter-actuator` supplies the
   `MeterRegistry`; auto-config builds a `MicrometerTelemetry` over it (decorated with
   `TracingTelemetry` when an `OpenTelemetry` bean is present — add
   `micrometer-tracing-bridge-otel` to opt in) and a `HealthIndicator` reporting the host
   UP with `activeSessions`/`mounts` at `/actuator/health`. The `pathland.*` meters are
   exposed at `/actuator/prometheus` (add `micrometer-registry-prometheus`).
 
 ## App DX
 
 ```java
 @SpringBootApplication
 public class MyApp {
     public static void main(String[] args) { SpringApplication.run(MyApp.class, args); }
     @Bean PathlandApp pathlandApp() { return () -> new MyHomeView(); }
     @Bean MountedApp support() { return MountedApp.of("/support", ...); } // optional 2nd app
 }
 ```
 
 ## Verified by
 
 `mvn test` — `PathlandAutoConfigurationTest` (`@SpringBootTest`): a `PathlandApp` bean
 mounts at `/` and SSR renders the root. `MultiSessionWebSocketTest`
 (`@SpringBootTest(RANDOM_PORT)`) opens **100 concurrent real WS sessions** against
 `/_pathland/ws` (via the shared `pathland-server-core` test-jar probe) and asserts each
 connects, re-syncs, gets transport-level PONGs, stays isolated, and is never closed by
 the peer. `PathlandObservabilityTest` (`@SpringBootTest` + `MockMvc`) asserts
 `/actuator/health` reports the `pathland` component UP and the auto-configured
 `PathlandTelemetry` is a `MicrometerTelemetry` registering `pathland.*` meters.
 `BaseCssHeadersTest` (`@SpringBootTest` + `MockMvc`) asserts the linked SSR
 `<link>`, the immutable `text/css` response at the global and mounted bases, and
 a 404 for an unknown hash.
 Manual: the `pathland-spring-boot-demo` renders `/`, `/kitchen`, `/settings`
 and the 404 fallback **and a second app at `/app2`**; a WebSocket handshake to
 `/_pathland/ws` and `/app2/_pathland/ws` returns 101.
\ No newline at end of file

+# Lettuce keeps Netty DNS resolver objects in static fields. Netty marks
+# DnsNameResolverBuilder for run-time initialization, while Quarkus initializes
+# application classes at build time; GraalVM then rejects the captured resolver
+# objects. Keep the three Lettuce holders run-time initialized. This metadata is
+# only on the classpath for apps that opt into Redis, so in-memory native builds
+# (e.g. the Quarkus demo) never see it.

+# pathland-state-redis — implementation status
+
+**Last updated:** November 8, 2026
+
+Opt-in Redis `StateStore` (Lettuce) for the Pathland server runtime. Kept out of
+`pathland-server-core` so deployments that use the in-memory store — and
+GraalVM native-image builds such as the Quarkus demo — never carry Lettuce.
+
+## Implemented
+
+- **`RedisStateStore`** (`dev.pathland.state.redis`): a `StateStore` backed by
+  Lettuce, storing Java-serialized values under plain keys. Supports a default
+  URI (`redis://localhost:6379`), an explicit `RedisURI`, or a caller-supplied
+  `RedisClient`.
+- **`RedisStateStores.redisOrFallback(fallback)`**: probes Redis once and returns
+  the Redis store when reachable, otherwise the supplied fallback (typically
+  `InMemoryStateStore`).
+- **`RedisStateStore.Provider`**: the framework-neutral `StateStoreProvider` SPI.
+- **Native-image metadata**: the module ships
+  `META-INF/native-image/.../native-image.properties`, keeping Lettuce's static
+  Netty DNS resolver holders run-time initialized. Apps that opt into Redis in a
+  native build get the workaround without app-level flags.
+
+## Usage
+
+```java
+@Produces @Singleton
+StateStore stateStore() {
+    return RedisStateStores.redisOrFallback(new InMemoryStateStore());
+}
+```
+
+Add the `pathland-state-redis` dependency and a `StateStore` bean; the Quarkus
+and Spring starters' default in-memory bean yields to it.
+
+## Not implemented / gaps
+
+- Java serialization of non-JDK state types in a native image still needs
+  reachability metadata for those types.
+- No automated Redis integration test (the store requires a live server); the
+  module builds and its provider/fallback seam is testable without one.

<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 http://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <parent>
        <groupId>dev.pathland</groupId>
        <artifactId>pathland-parent</artifactId>
        <version>0.2.2</version>
    </parent>

    <artifactId>pathland-state-redis</artifactId>
    <packaging>jar</packaging>

    <name>Pathland State Redis</name>
    <description>
        Opt-in Redis StateStore (Lettuce) for the Pathland server runtime. Kept out of
        pathland-server-core so server deployments that use the in-memory store — and
        GraalVM native-image builds such as the Quarkus demo — never carry Lettuce.
        Apps add this module and provide a StateStore bean when they want Redis.
    </description>

    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>dev.pathland</groupId>
            <artifactId>pathland-view-core</artifactId>
            <version>${project.version}</version>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>io.lettuce</groupId>
            <artifactId>lettuce-core</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.slf4j</groupId>
            <artifactId>slf4j-api</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
            <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
            <scope>test</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

    <build>
        <plugins>
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
                <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>

# Lettuce keeps Netty DNS resolver objects in static fields. Netty marks
# DnsNameResolverBuilder for run-time initialization, while Quarkus initializes
# application classes at build time; GraalVM then rejects the captured resolver
# objects. Keep the three Lettuce holders run-time initialized. This metadata is
# only on the classpath for apps that opt into Redis, so in-memory native builds
# (e.g. the Quarkus demo) never see it.
Args = --initialize-at-run-time=io.lettuce.core.resource.DefaultClientResources \
       --initialize-at-run-time=io.lettuce.core.resource.AddressResolverGroupProvider \
       --initialize-at-run-time=io.lettuce.core.resource.AddressResolverGroupProvider$DefaultDnsAddressResolverGroupWrapper

# --- Native image (GraalVM/Mandrel) ---------------------------------------------
# The starter probes Redis at startup via Lettuce. Lettuce keeps a Netty
# DnsAddressResolverGroup (built from a DnsNameResolverBuilder) in static fields,
# and Netty marks that builder for run-time initialization. Quarkus initializes
# application classes at build time, so those resolver objects would land in the
# image heap and GraalVM rejects them. Keep the three Lettuce holder classes

input.content:
# pathland-state-redis — implementation status

**Last updated:** November 8, 2026

Opt-in Redis `StateStore` (Lettuce) for the Pathland server runtime. Kept out of
`pathland-server-core` so deployments that use the in-memory store — and
GraalVM native-image builds such as the Quarkus demo — never carry Lettuce.

## Implemented

- **`RedisStateStore`** (`dev.pathland.state.redis`): a `StateStore` backed by
  Lettuce, storing Java-serialized values under plain keys. Supports a default
  URI (`redis://localhost:6379`), an explicit `RedisURI`, or a caller-supplied
  `RedisClient`.
- **`RedisStateStores.redisOrFallback(fallback)`**: probes Redis once and returns
  the Redis store when reachable, otherwise the supplied fallback (typically
  `InMemoryStateStore`).
- **`RedisStateStore.Provider`**: the framework-neutral `StateStoreProvider` SPI.
- **Native-image metadata**: the module ships
  `META-INF/native-image/.../native-image.properties`, keeping Lettuce's static
  Netty DNS resolver holders run-time initialized. Apps that opt into Redis in a
  native build get the workaround without app-level flags.

## Usage

```java
@Produces @Singleton
StateStore stateStore() {
    return RedisStateStores.redisOrFallback(new InMemoryStateStore());
}
```

Add the `pathland-state-redis` dependency and a `StateStore` bean; the Quarkus
and Spring starters' default in-memory bean yields to it.

## Not implemented / gaps

- Java serialization of non-JDK state types in a native image still needs
  reachability metadata for those types.
- No automated Redis integration test (the store requires a live server); the
  module builds and its provider/fallback seam is testable without one.

# pathland-server-core — implementation status

**Last updated:** November 7, 2026

The transport-agnostic Pathland server runtime: one app instance per session (SSR +
live 16-byte opcode deltas + environment), the session registry, and the **multi-app
host** (the BFF), shared by the Spring Boot and Quarkus starters. No web-framework
dependency — framework glue lives in the starters.

## Implemented

- **Security hardening (issue #63)**: `WindowIds` validates the client-supplied

The service worker does a network fetch with `cache: "reload"` and `redirect: "manual"`, and does `await widFor(event)` which involves `caches.open` + `cache.match` before fetching. That adds some latency, but likely not 500ms. The key clue: Chrome says 524ms for the first full response. Curl 63ms. The service worker on first load:
- The page initially loads from network (SW not controlling yet), then registers the SW. On `install`, `skipWaiting`; on `activate`, `clients.claim()`. The first page is uncontrolled; after `clients.claim`, the SW controls the page. Then the user might reload or navigate. The SW intercepts the navigation, does `widFor(event)` (Cache API open/match) + `fetch` with `cache: "reload"`.
- `cache: "reload"` bypasses the HTTP cache and forces a network fetch. This is intentional to avoid stale SSR body. It might cause the request to go to the server and take 500ms? But curl to server is 63ms. The SW fetch with `cache: "reload"` adds request headers maybe `Pragma: no-cache`, `Cache-Control: no-cache`, causing the server to do more work? The server is a native Quarkus app; no caching. Should still be ~63ms. 524ms might include SW startup (cold start) + Cache API + fetch + HTML parse? Chrome's timing "first full response" maybe includes the document load, not just server response. If the HTML is large (the music player SSR with many nodes, inline CSS? The CSS is linked, not inline; the DOM renderer bundle is a script). The "first full response" 524ms might include:
  - SW cold start (starting the worker thread) ~50-100ms
  - `caches.open` + `cache.match` ~ few ms
  - network fetch ~63ms
  - downloading HTML body (maybe 100-300KB?) over localhost ~ fast
  - Chrome's "first full response" might be from navigation start to response complete, including SW startup.

But 524ms is suspicious. Could be the native container under x86 emulation? Curl 63ms to the same container. The SW fetch goes through the browser network stack, which might resolve `localhost` to IPv6 `::1` first, fail, then fall back to IPv4, adding latency? Curl also uses localhost. Chrome might try IPv6 `::1` and the container only maps IPv4? Docker publishes both? On macOS Docker Desktop, `localhost:8080` maps to both? Curl 63ms suggests fine. Chrome may have a 300ms DNS/connection delay due to proxy settings or IPv6. But the user specifically says "through the serviceworker", implying they compared with SW disabled and saw faster. Need to ask or analyze.

We should inspect the service worker and understand its overhead. Potential improvements:
1. Avoid `cache: "reload"` on every navigation? It forces network, but the server is local. The intent is to avoid stale SSR. The rewritten URL includes `?wid=...`, which is a distinct cache key, so HTTP cache wouldn't have a stale entry for the same URL except on reload. `cache: "reload"` is only needed for same-window reload; it forces a full revalidation. Could use `cache: "no-cache"` instead? `no-cache` still validates with the server. The server may not send validators. `reload` is fine.
2. The SW does `widFor` before `fetch`, which is async Cache API. Could be optimized by caching the wid in memory? The SW can be evicted, but during a session it stays. Use an in-memory map as a fast path, fall back to Cache API. That could shave a few ms, not 500.
3. The first load after SW install: the SW isn't controlling the initial page; the user reloads, and the SW starts. The first SW-controlled navigation includes worker startup. Chrome's 524ms could be the first controlled navigation, including SW startup. Subsequent navigations should be faster. We can ask the user to check the second/third navigation timing. If the 524ms is only the first, it's SW cold start, not a real issue.
4. Chrome DevTools may attribute the SW startup to the navigation timing. The SW's `install`/`activate`/`clients.claim` happen after the first page load, not during the first navigation. The second navigation's SW startup may be ~50-100ms, not 500.
5. Another big factor: the HTML response is not compressed? If the SSR HTML is large (maybe 100KB+) and the server doesn't gzip, Chrome's network stack might take longer than curl? Curl on localhost is fast even uncompressed. 524ms could be Chrome's "first full response" including `DOMContentLoaded`? Need to clarify what Chrome metric they're reading. Chrome DevTools Network tab "Waiting for server response" vs "Content Download" vs "Finish". The "first full response" might be the "Finish" time, which includes the response body download. If the HTML is large and the SW `fetch` response is streamed through the SW, the SW may buffer the response? The SW returns the `Response` directly, so it streams. But the browser's SW fetch may have overhead.
6. Could the SW be doing `await remember(event.resultingClientId, wid)` before returning the response? In the code, it does `await remember(...)` after `fetch` and before `return response`. This adds a Cache API `put` operation to the critical path of every navigation! That could be tens of ms, maybe more on first use. The `remember` after fetch is not needed before returning the response; it can be done in the background with `event.waitUntil`. This is a likely culprit. The SW awaits `remember` (cache.put) before returning the HTML response. On a cold cache, `caches.open` + `cache.put` can be slow (disk I/O, maybe 100-500ms). That would explain 524ms! The initial `widFor` also does `caches.open`/`cache.match`, but `remember` after fetch is an extra write on the critical path. We should recommend moving `remember` to `event.waitUntil(...)` or not awaiting it. The `fetch` handler's `respondWith` promise resolves only after `remember` completes. So the browser waits for the Cache API write before it gets the response. That's a real performance bug.

Let's confirm: In `sw.js`:
```js
const response = await fetch(...);
await remember(event.resultingClientId, wid);
return response;
```
Yes. This is on the critical path. It should be:
```js
const response = await fetch(...);
event.waitUntil(remember(event.resultingClientId, wid));
return response;
```
But `event.waitUntil` can be called inside the `respondWith` async function? Yes, `event.waitUntil` can be called during the fetch event dispatch; it extends the event lifetime. However, once `respondWith` has been called, `event.waitUntil` can still be called? The spec allows `waitUntil` during the event dispatch, including inside the async function before the promise settles. It should work. Alternatively, fire-and-forget `void remember(...)` (but the worker may be terminated before it completes; `waitUntil` is safer).
- Similarly, `widFor` does `await recall` before the network fetch. That's necessary to build the URL. Could use an in-memory cache to speed it up.
- The `message` handler uses `event.waitUntil(remember(...))` already. Good.
- The fetch handler's `remember` is the likely culprit.

Also, the SW `fetch` uses `cache: "reload"`, which bypasses HTTP cache. That's intentional but adds network. On localhost, not 500ms.

Another possible critical path: `widFor` calls `self.clients.matchAll` only when `event.clientId` is empty (Safari). Chrome has clientId, so it does `recall` (Cache API read) before fetch. Cache API read can be ~1-10ms, not 500ms. But if the Cache API is cold, maybe more. Still, the write is likely bigger.

We should read the service-worker tests to see if they assert the `remember` ordering. The e2e test only checks the wid is attached. We can propose a test.

Also, the `service-worker.ts` registration code: `navigator.serviceWorker.register` runs on every page load (in `ms()` after DOM boot). It registers the SW and posts the wid. The `post()` is called immediately, and again on `updatefound`, `ready`, `controllerchange`. Fine.

Another potential issue: The SW `install` handler does `self.skipWaiting()`, and `activate` does `clients.claim()`. On first load, the page is claimed after activation. Then `setupServiceWorker` posts the wid. On the next navigation, the SW is active. The 524ms might be the first navigation after SW activation, including SW startup. But the `remember` write is still on the critical path.

We should also consider that Chrome's "first full response" might be the "Waiting for server response" time. If it's 524ms, the SW's `await remember` happens after the fetch response is received, so it would show under "Content Download" or "Finish", not "Waiting for server response". The user says "first full response of the html", likely "Finish" or "Load". We need to ask which Chrome metric. But we can explain both.

We should present an analysis and a plan:
1. Explain the SW is pass-through but adds two async Cache API operations per navigation: `recall` before fetch (necessary) and `remember` after fetch (not necessary on the critical path).
2. The `await remember(event.resultingClientId, wid)` before `return response` delays the HTML response by the Cache API write. Move it off the critical path via `event.waitUntil(remember(...))` or fire-and-forget.
3. Optionally add an in-memory `Map<clientId, wid>` fast path in the worker to avoid `caches.open`/`match` on every navigation; use Cache API as persistence/fallback.
4. `cache: "reload"` forces a network fetch on every navigation; that's intentional for SSR freshness, but it means the SW can't serve from HTTP cache. If the server is local, fine. If the user wants faster repeat navigations, consider `cache: "no-cache"` (revalidate) or only `reload` on actual reloads. But the primary fix is the write.
5. Verify with Chrome DevTools: compare timings with SW enabled/disabled, first vs subsequent navigation, and look at the Network panel breakdown. Use `performance.getEntriesByType("navigation")[0]` for TTFB/response times. Check whether 524ms is SW startup on first controlled load vs steady-state.
6. Add an e2e/unit test that the fetch handler resolves the response before the `remember` write completes (e.g., mock a slow `cache.put` and assert the response promise resolves without waiting). This prevents regression.

We should also inspect whether the service worker's `fetch` handler is in the demo's bundled `dom-renderer` and whether the `sw.js` is copied. The source `lib/typescript/sw.js` is the worker; the Java resources are copies. The fix would be in `lib/typescript/sw.js`, then `npm run build:all`/copy script to update the demo resources. The user is in plan mode; we should mention the change flow.

We need to know the build/copy script: `lib/typescript/scripts/copy-to-libs.mjs` copies `sw.js` to Java resources. Let's inspect quickly to plan.

Title: Navigation Preload: Faster Service Worker Navigations - Progressive Web Apps
URL: https://progressivewebapps.com/service-workers/navigation-preload/
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
Navigation preload lets the browser start a navigation's network request at the same time as it boots your service worker, instead of waiting for the worker to start and run its `fetch` handler first. The worker then picks up the in-flight response from `event.preloadResponse`. For sites that answer navigations from the network (network-first, or streamed pages), it removes worker start-up from the most latency-sensitive request you have, and it is supported in Chromium, Firefox and Safari.

Key takeaways

- Without preload, a cold service worker delays every navigation it handles: web.dev puts boot-up at usually around 50 ms, more like 250 ms on mobile, and over 500 ms in extreme cases.
- Enable it with `self.registration.navigationPreload.enable()` in the `activate` event, then use `await event.preloadResponse` instead of `fetch(event.request)` for navigations.
- The preload request is the navigation request plus a `Service-Worker-Navigation-Preload` header (default value `true`, changeable with `setHeaderValue()`); servers that vary their response on it must send `Vary: Service-Worker-Navigation-Preload`.
- Preload only applies to `GET` navigations (pages and iframes), and its state lives on the registration, so it persists across worker updates until something calls `disable()`.
- If you enable it and then answer from the cache without touching `preloadResponse`, you waste a request and Chromium warns; if you also call `fetch(event.request)`, you make the request twice.
- It is the wrong tool for app-shell sites that always answer navigations from the cache.
- Supported in Chrome 59, Firefox 99 and Safari 15.4 and later.

...

When a page is controlled by a service worker with a `fetch` listener, the browser cannot send the navigation request until the worker has decided what to do with it. If the worker is not running, the browser must first start it: create a thread, evaluate your script, run any top-level code, and then dispatch the `fetch` event. Only then can your handler call `fetch()`.

...

Jake Archibald's web.dev article that introduced the feature says boot-up is "usually around 50ms", "more like 250ms" on mobile, and "in extreme cases (slow devices, CPU in distress) it can be over 500ms". Because the browser keeps a worker alive for a while between events, you only pay it occasionally, but "occasionally" is exactly the first navigation of a visit: arriving from a search result, opening a bookmark, tapping a home-screen icon. Chromium stops an idle worker after about 30 seconds without events, so most first navigations of a session start cold.

Title: Handling navigation requests  |  Articles  |  web.dev
URL: https://web.dev/articles/handling-navigation-requests
Published: N/A
Author: Jeff Posnick X GitHub Homepage
Highlights:
Navigation requests are requests for HTML documents made by your browser whenever you enter a new URL in the navigation bar, or follow a link on a page taking you to a new URL. This is where service workers make their biggest impact on performance: if you use a service worker to respond to navigation requests without waiting for the network, you can ensure that navigations are reliably fast, in addition to being resilient when the network is unavailable. This is the single biggest performance win that comes from a service worker, versus what's possible with HTTP caching.

...

Inside of a service worker's `fetch` event handler, you can determine whether a request is a navigation by checking the `request.mode` property on the `FetchEvent`. If it's set to `'navigate'`, then it's a navigation request.

As a general rule, do not use long-lived `Cache-Control headers` to cache the HTML response for a navigation request. They should normally be satisfied via the network, with `Cache-Control: no-cache`, to ensure that the HTML, along with the chain of subsequent network requests, is (reasonably) fresh. Going against the network each time the user navigates to a new page unfortunately means that each navigation might be slow. At the very least, it means that it won't be reliably fast.

Note: `Cache-Control: no-cache` means the browser must check (or "revalidate") with the server before using a previously cached resource. This requires a round-trip network communication to complete before the resource can be used.

...

### Everything else

If you can't respond to navigation requests with cached HTML, you must take steps to ensure that adding a service worker to your site (to handle other, non-HTML requests) doesn't end up slowing down your navigations. Starting up the service worker without using it to respond to a navigation request will introduce a small amount of latency (as explained in Building Faster, More Resilient Apps with Service Worker). You can mitigate this overhead by enabling a feature called navigation preload, and then using the network response that's been preloaded inside of your `fetch` event handler.

Workbox provides a helper library that feature-detects whether navigation preload is supported, and if so, simplifies the process of telling your service worker to use the network response.

Title: Slow service-worker cache on IOS
URL: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/69108997/slow-service-worker-cache-on-ios
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
To serve content from the cache and make your app available offline you need to intercept the network requests and respond with files stored in the cache. There are several approaches to this as per this documentation :

cache only
network only
cache falling back to network
network falling back to cache
cache then network

Actually, what you are doing is serving the content using cache falling back to the network strategy by using the code below :
event.respondWith( caches.match(event.request)
.then(function(response) { 
return response || fetch(event.request); 
})

which works like "Cache only" behavior for things in the cache and the "Network only" behaviour for anything not cached”, but rather what you want to use is either network falling back to the cache or cache then network strategy.
Network Falling back to Cache :
From the documentation,

Handling network requests this way means the online users get the most
up-to-date content, and offline users get an older cached version.
However, this method has flaws. If the user has an intermittent or
slow connection they'll have to wait for the network to fail before
they get content from the cache.

Unlike caches.match in your cache falling back to network strategy here we first send the request to the network using fetch(), and only if it fails do we look for a response in the cache.
Cache then network :
From the documentation,

This requires the page to make two requests: one to the cache, and one
to the network. The idea is to show the cached data first, then update
the page when/if the network data arrives.

Meaning : It will serve the content from cache immediately and then update the content as soon as the latest response is available via the n/w call. This is the most recommended strategy,
The problem in serving content from your current strategy is we are reading the cache content via e.respondWith(caches.match(e.request).then(function(response) but the update is happening via e.waitUntil(update(e.request)) in the next pass until the network call is completed which is not even used in this current read request.
So my suggestion is to increase the performance of the service workers by using the Cache then network strategy.

## Summary

Aligns the [Create Fetch Event and Dispatch](https://w3c.github.io/ServiceWorker/#create-fetch-event-and-dispatch-algorithm) algorithm and the `FetchEvent.clientId` / `resultingClientId` attribute definitions with **actual browser behavior** (Chrome, Firefox, Safari) and MDN.

Fixes #1267.

## Changes

### 1. `FetchEvent.clientId` algorithm step

Previously the spec unconditionally initialized `clientId` from `request`'s client, including for navigations. However, all major browsers return an empty string for `clientId` on navigation requests. Per [@wanderview's suggestion](https://github.com/w3c/ServiceWorker/issues/1267#issuecomment-362298501):

> My inclination is to probably implement resultingClientId and keep navigation clientId empty at first.

**Before:**
> If |client| is not null, initialize |e|'s clientId attribute to |client|'s environment id.

**After:**
> If |request| is a subresource request and |client| is not null, initialize |e|'s clientId attribute to |client|'s environment id.

### 2. `FetchEvent.resultingClientId` algorithm step

Adds an explicit `reservedClient` null check and removes the redundant "and to the empty string otherwise" clause (the IDL default already provides `""`).

### 3. `FetchEvent.replacesClientId` algorithm step

Removes the redundant "and to the empty string otherwise" clause for consistency with the sibling attributes.

### 4. Explanatory notes

Added descriptive notes for both `FetchEvent.clientId` and `FetchEvent.resultingClientId` attribute sections, documenting all cases where the value is the empty string. These match MDN's documented behavior.

state.title: Exa Web Search: Safari service worker event.clientId empty navigation resultingClientId

parts.text:
We now have a strong explanation: Safari's navigation `clientId` is empty (as spec/WebKit), so `widFor` falls into `self.clients.matchAll`, which in Safari is an IPC that can be slow. Chrome also has empty `clientId` for navigations according to the search, but the code comment says Chrome reports the initiating document's client id; the search says all major browsers return empty for navigations (per 2026 spec clarification). Hmm, the search says "all major browsers return an empty string for clientId on navigation requests" (July 2026 spec PR). If Chrome also empty, then Chrome would also call `clients.matchAll` and be fast. Safari's `matchAll` may be slower. Also Safari may not expose `resultingClientId` (older Safari), but modern Safari does. The code uses `event.clientId` only.

The 524ms Safari vs 34-70ms Chrome suggests Safari's service worker startup + `clients.matchAll` + Cache API are slower. The fix should reduce the critical path and possibly avoid `clients.matchAll` in Safari.

Let's think about how to avoid `clients.matchAll`:
- The worker can maintain an in-memory map of known clients from `postMessage` events (the page sends its wid on boot). The `event.source.id` gives the client id. On a navigation with empty `clientId`, if there's exactly one known client, use its wid. If multiple, we need to disambiguate. But Safari's `clients.matchAll` is the only authoritative way.
- However, we can use `event.resultingClientId`? The wid is stored under the old client id, not the new. The worker could store a mapping from `resultingClientId` → wid after each navigation. On the next navigation, the initiating document's id is the previous `resultingClientId`, but `event.clientId` is empty, so we don't know which previous resulting id is navigating. Unless we can get it from `event.replacesClientId`? There is `replacesClientId` in the spec: "the id of the client that replaces the previous client during a page navigation." For a navigation from page A to B, `replacesClientId` is A's client id, and `resultingClientId` is B's client id. Is `replacesClientId` exposed in Safari? The spec mentions it, but browser support may be limited. If Safari supports `replacesClientId`, the worker could use it directly to recall the wid stored under A's id. This would avoid `clients.matchAll` entirely. Let's check `FetchEvent.replacesClientId` support. MDN? It's part of the spec; maybe Chrome/Firefox support it, Safari? Search.

```
## Summary

Aligns the [Create Fetch Event and Dispatch](https://w3c.github.io/ServiceWorker/#create-fetch-event-and-dispatch-algorithm) algorithm and the `FetchEvent.clientId` / `resultingClientId` attribute definitions with **actual browser behavior** (Chrome, Firefox, Safari) and MDN.

Fixes #1267.

## Changes

### 1. `FetchEvent.clientId` algorithm step

Previously the spec unconditionally initialized `clientId` from `request`'s client, including for navigations. However, all major browsers return an empty string for `clientId` on navigation requests. Per [@wanderview's suggestion](https://github.com/w3c/ServiceWorker/issues/1267#issuecomment-362298501):

> My inclination is to probably implement resultingClientId and keep navigation clientId empty at first.

**Before:**
> If |client| is not null, initialize |e|'s clientId attribute to |client|'s environment id.

**After:**
> If |request| is a subresource request and |client| is not null, initialize |e|'s clientId attribute to |client|'s environment id.

### 2. `FetchEvent.resultingClientId` algorithm step

Adds an explicit `reservedClient` null check and removes the redundant "and to the empty string otherwise" clause (the IDL default already provides `""`).

### 3. `FetchEvent.replacesClientId` algorithm step

Removes the redundant "and to the empty string otherwise" clause for consistency with the sibling attributes.

### 4. Explanatory notes

Added descriptive notes for both `FetchEvent.clientId` and `FetchEvent.resultingClientId` attribute sections, documenting all cases where the value is the empty string. These match MDN's documented behavior.

Title: Speed up service worker with navigation preloads  |  Blog  |  web.dev
URL: https://web.dev/blog/navigation-preload
Published: N/A
Author: Jake Archibald X Homepage
Highlights:
Navigation preload lets you overcome service worker startup time by making requests in parallel.

 Jake Archibald 

Browser Support

- 59 
- 18 
- 99 
- 15.4 

## Summary

- In some situations, service worker boot-up time can delay a network response.
- Available in the three major browser engines, navigation preload fixes this by allowing you to make the request in parallel with service worker boot-up.
- You can distinguish preload requests from regular navigations using a header, and serve different content.

## The problem

When you navigate to a site that uses a service worker to handle fetch events, the browser asks the service worker for a response. This involves booting up the service worker (if it isn't already running), and dispatching the fetch event.

The bootup time depends on the device and conditions. It's usually around 50ms. On mobile it's more like 250ms. In extreme cases (slow devices, CPU in distress) it can be over 500ms. However, since the service worker stays awake for a browser-determined time between events, you only get this delay occasionally, such as when the user navigates to your site from a fresh tab, or another site.

The boot-up time isn't a problem if you're responding from the cache, as the benefit of skipping the network is greater than the boot-up delay. But if you're responding using the network…

SW boot Navigation request

The network request is delayed by the service worker booting-up.

We're continuing to reduce the boot-up time by using code-caching in V8, by skipping service workers that don't have a fetch event, by launching service workers speculatively, and other optimizations. However, bootup time will always be greater than zero.

Facebook brought the impact of this problem to our attention, and asked for a way to perform navigation requests in parallel:

## Navigation preload to the rescue

Navigation preload is a feature that lets you say, "When the user makes a GET navigation request, start the network request while the service worker is booting up".

The startup delay is still there, but it doesn't block the network request, so the user gets content sooner.

Here's a video of it in action, where the service worker is given a deliberate 500ms startup delay using a while-loop:

Here's the demo itself. To get the benefits of navigation preload, you'll need a browser that supports it.

## Activate navigation preload

...

addEventListener('activate', event => {
  event.waitUntil(async function() {
    // Feature-detect
    if (self.registration.navigationPreload) {
      // Enable navigation preloads!
      await self.registration.navigationPreload.enable();
    }
  }());
});

```

You can call `navigationPreload.enable()` whenever you want, or disable it with `navigationPreload.disable()`. However, since your `fetch` event needs to make use of it, it's best to enable and disable it in your service worker's `activate` event.

...

Now the browser will be performing preloads for navigations, but you still need to use the response:

```
addEventListener('fetch', event => {
  event.respondWith(async function() {
    // Respond from the cache if we can
    const cachedResponse = await caches.match(event.request);
    if (cachedResponse) return cachedResponse;

    // Else, use the preloaded response, if it's there
    const response = await event.preloadResponse;
    if (response) return response;

    // Else try the network.
    return fetch(event.request);
  }());
});

```

`event.preloadResponse` is a promise that resolves with a response, if:

- Navigation preload is enabled.
- The request is a `GET` request.
- The request is a navigation request (which browsers generate when they're loading pages, including iframes).

Otherwise `event.preloadResponse` is still there, but it resolves with `undefined`.

...

However, the request for `includeURL` will be delayed by the service worker's startup time. We can use navigation preload to fix this too, but in this case we don't want to preload the full page, we want to preload an include.

To support this, a header is sent with every preload request:

```
Service-Worker-Navigation-Preload: true

```

The server can use this to send different content for navigation preload requests than it would for a regular navigation request. Just remember to add a `Vary: Service-Worker-Navigation-Preload` header, so caches know that your responses differ.

Title: Navigation Preload: Faster Service Worker Navigations - Progressive Web Apps
URL: https://progressivewebapps.com/service-workers/navigation-preload/
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
# Navigation Preload¶

Navigation preload lets the browser start a navigation's network request at the same time as it boots your service worker, instead of waiting for the worker to start and run its `fetch` handler first. The worker then picks up the in-flight response from `event.preloadResponse`. For sites that answer navigations from the network (network-first, or streamed pages), it removes worker start-up from the most latency-sensitive request you have, and it is supported in Chromium, Firefox and Safari.

Key takeaways

- Without preload, a cold service worker delays every navigation it handles: web.dev puts boot-up at usually around 50 ms, more like 250 ms on mobile, and over 500 ms in extreme cases.
- Enable it with `self.registration.navigationPreload.enable()` in the `activate` event, then use `await event.preloadResponse` instead of `fetch(event.request)` for navigations.
- The preload request is the navigation request plus a `Service-Worker-Navigation-Preload` header (default value `true`, changeable with `setHeaderValue()`); servers that vary their response on it must send `Vary: Service-Worker-Navigation-Preload`.
- Preload only applies to `GET` navigations (pages and iframes), and its state lives on the registration, so it persists across worker updates until something calls `disable()`.
- If you enable it and then answer from the cache without touching `preloadResponse`, you waste a request and Chromium warns; if you also call `fetch(event.request)`, you make the request twice.
- It is the wrong tool for app-shell sites that always answer navigations from the cache.
- Supported in Chrome 59, Firefox 99 and Safari 15.4 and later.

...

When a page is controlled by a service worker with a `fetch` listener, the browser cannot send the navigation request until the worker has decided what to do with it.

...

Jake Archibald's web.dev article that introduced the feature says boot-up is "usually around 50ms", "more like 250ms" on mobile, and "in extreme cases (slow devices, CPU in distress) it can be over 500ms". Because the browser keeps a worker alive for a while between events, you only pay it occasionally, but "occasionally" is exactly the first navigation of a visit: arriving from a search result, opening a bookmark, tapping a home-screen icon. Chromium stops an idle worker after about 30 seconds without events, so most first navigations of a session start cold.

...

| Phase | Depends on | Overlapped by preload? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Worker thread and script start-up | Device CPU, script size, top-level work | Yes |
| `fetch` event dispatch | Number of listeners, code before `respondWith()` | Yes |
| Your handler's work before the network request (cache lookups, IndexedDB reads) | Your code | Yes, if you start from `preloadResponse` |
| DNS, connection, TLS, request, server think time, first byte | Network and server | This is the preload |

...

## Browser support¶

Support data as of September 2026. For live data, see MDN's NavigationPreloadManager compatibility table and FetchEvent.preloadResponse.

| Feature | Chrome / Edge | Firefox | Safari (macOS and iOS) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ServiceWorkerRegistration.navigationPreload` | ✅ 59 | ✅ 99 | ✅ 15.4 |
| `enable()`, `disable()`, `getState()` | ✅ 59 | ✅ 99 | ✅ 15.4 |
| `setHeaderValue()` | ✅ 59 | ✅ 99 | ⚠️ 15.4 |
| `FetchEvent.preloadResponse` | ✅ 59 | ✅ 99 | ✅ 15.4 |
| Automatic preload without opting in (ServiceWorkerAutoPreload) | ⚠️ | ❌ | ❌ |

⚠️ Safari 15.4 shipped without sending the `Service-Worker-Navigation-Preload` header on preload requests (WebKit bug 238564, fixed in WebKit in April 2022), so servers could not recognize preload requests from that release. The preload itself worked. ⚠️ ServiceWorkerAutoPreload is an optional Chromium optimization applied at the browser's discretion, not a web-exposed API.

Edge 18 (EdgeHTML) also implemented navigation preload; every Chromium-based Edge version (79 and later) matches Chrome. Because all current engines support it, feature detection (`if (self.registration.navigationPreload)`) is now mostly about older installed browsers and embedded web views.

# Service-Worker-Navigation-Preload header

 Limited availability 

This feature is not Baseline because it does not work in some of the most widely-used browsers.

- See full compatibility 
- Learn more 

The HTTP `Service-Worker-Navigation-Preload` request header indicates that the request was the result of a `fetch()` operation made during service worker navigation preloading. It allows a server to respond with a different resource than for a normal `fetch()`.

If a different response may result from setting this header, the server must include a `Vary: Service-Worker-Navigation-Preload` header in responses to ensure that different responses are cached.

For more information see `NavigationPreloadManager.setHeaderValue()` (and `NavigationPreloadManager`).

The following request header is sent by default in navigation preload requests:

http

```
Service-Worker-Navigation-Preload: true

Service-Worker-Navigation-Preload: json_fragment1

Now we have strong info:
- Safari's SW boot-up can be >500ms in extreme cases; Safari's SW startup is likely slower. Chrome 34-70ms.
- Navigation preload can eliminate the SW startup delay for navigations. Safari supports it (15.4+). But the worker needs to rewrite the URL with `?wid=...`; navigation preload preloads the original request (without wid). If we use `event.preloadResponse`, we'd get the unscoped SSR, not the wid-scoped one. Could we use navigation preload and still add the wid? The preload request is the original navigation URL; the SW can't modify it. We could add the wid via a header `Service-Worker-Navigation-Preload`? The server could read a custom header? The SW can set the preload header value via `navigationPreload.setHeaderValue(wid)`, but the header value is set on the registration, not per-request, and it's shared across tabs. Also the server would need to read `Service-Worker-Navigation-Preload` as the wid. But the wid is per-tab; `setHeaderValue` is global to the registration. Not suitable.
- Alternatively, the SW can use navigation preload for the initial request and then still fetch the rewritten URL? That doubles requests. Not good.
- Could the server accept the wid from a header set by the SW? The SW can't set headers on the navigation request before it's sent; navigation preload is the only way to start early. So no.
- The 524ms in Safari may be SW startup (cold). Navigation preload would hide it, but we can't use it because of the wid rewrite. Unless we change the architecture: instead of rewriting the URL in the SW, have the server read the wid from a cookie? Not per-tab. Or use a request header set by the page? The page can't set headers on navigation. Or use a `sessionStorage`-backed id in the URL? The id must not appear in the address bar. The SW rewrite is the chosen design.
- Another option: avoid the SW for the initial navigation and accept default SSR, then correct via WS (current behavior when SW is off). The SW is an optimization for first-paint persisted state. Safari users pay 500ms for it. We could feature-detect Safari and skip the SW? That would lose the first-paint state scope on Safari, but the live connection corrects it. The user may prefer that. Or make the SW opt-in per browser? The server sets `data-pathland-service-worker` globally. Could the client skip registration on Safari? The SW is already installed; the client could unregister on Safari. But the server's SSR would still be unscoped until WS. That's the pre-SW behavior. This is a tradeoff.
- Or improve the SW so Safari's cost is lower:
  1. Move `await remember` off the critical path.
  2. Avoid `clients.matchAll` when possible. Safari's `clients.matchAll` may be the main cost; can we use a cached client ID? The page posts its wid with `event.source.id`; the worker can keep an in-memory map of known client IDs. If there's exactly one known client, use it. If multiple, fall back to `clients.matchAll`. On Safari, with one tab, this avoids the `matchAll` call. But if the page reloads, the client ID changes; the worker gets a new postMessage after the new page loads. The first navigation after a fresh tab still has no known client? The page posted its wid after the first load; the worker has the client id. On the next navigation, the in-memory map has one entry → use it. This avoids `matchAll`. If the user opens a second tab, the map has two entries; fall back to `matchAll` to disambiguate. This is a solid optimization.
  3. Keep the in-memory map for wid values, avoiding Cache API reads/writes on the critical path. Use Cache API for persistence across worker restarts.
  4. The SW still boots on navigation; Safari's cold start remains. But the user's 524ms may be mostly `matchAll` + Cache API, not boot. We can measure.
- Another optimization: Use `event.resultingClientId` to store the wid after the response, and on the next navigation, use `clients.get`? Not helpful.
- Another idea: use `self.clients.matchAll({ type: "window", includeUncontrolled: false })` to reduce the set. The current `includeUncontrolled: true` may include more clients and be slower. After `clients.claim()`, the page is controlled. On the first navigation after install, the current page might be uncontrolled; but the worker is active and claims it. `includeUncontrolled: false` would exclude the old uncontrolled client, causing the navigation to fail open. Hmm.
- Another idea: use `event.request.url` and a URL→wid map. If there's one tab, map the URL to wid. On navigation from A to B, the initiating URL is the referrer, not the target. The worker could store `wid` under the current URL and use `event.request.referrer` to look up. The referrer is available in the fetch event. This avoids `clients.matchAll`:
  - On each page load, the page posts its wid and its URL; the worker stores `url → wid`.
  - On a navigation, `event.request.referrer` is the current page URL (usually). Look up the wid by referrer. If found, use it. If multiple tabs at the same URL with different wids, ambiguous; fall back to `matchAll` or fail open.
  - This is clever but fragile (referrer policies, `no-referrer`). The SW could also store the wid under the client id and use `event.request.referrer` as a hint. Not robust.
- The in-memory known-clients map is simpler and robust enough:
  - `message` handler: `knownWids.set(event.source.id, data.wid)` and `knownClients.set(event.source.id, {wid, url: ...})`.

    - else → `clients.matchAll` and disambiguate by URL.

We should ask if subsequent navigations are also 524ms or only the first. If only the first, the fix is navigation preload (not compatible with wid rewrite) or accept the cold start; if every navigation, the in-memory map + critical-path fix will help a lot.

- Safari-specific because WebKit leaves `event.clientId` empty for navigations (spec-compliant; all browsers do per 2026, but the code's comment says Chrome sets it; regardless, Safari hits the `clients.matchAll` fallback). The fallback enumerates window clients (IPC) on every navigation, then does Cache API read/write, then network. Safari's SW startup is also slower.
- Chrome's 34-70ms suggests the server is fine.
- The concrete fixes:
  1. Move `await remember` to `event.waitUntil` (not blocking response).
  2. Add an in-memory `Map<clientId, wid>` and a single-client fast path to avoid `clients.matchAll` in the common one-tab case.
  3. Use the in-memory map for `recall` before Cache API.
  4. Optional: `clients.matchAll` with `includeUncontrolled: false` after claim? Not sure; maybe keep.
  5. Optional: navigation preload is the proper fix for SW cold start, but it can't carry the `wid` rewrite. We could discuss a different mechanism for the wid (e.g., a per-tab cookie? Not per-tab; a header? Can't). So navigation preload isn't directly applicable unless we change how the wid reaches the server. This is a design tradeoff.
  6. Consider skipping the SW on Safari if first-paint state scoping is not worth 500ms. The live WS corrects state after connect. Could feature-detect Safari in `service-worker.ts` and unregister/skip. This is a product decision.
- Diagnostic: ask if 524ms is first navigation only; check Safari Web Inspector → Network → document timing; check SW console; compare after second navigation. Also test with `pathland.service-worker=false` (requires rebuild) or unregistering the SW in Safari settings. Also check Safari's SW startup time via Web Inspector timeline.
- Plan: implement the safe optimizations (1-3), add tests, rebuild. Then measure. If cold start remains, discuss disabling on Safari or a different wid transport.

We need to be careful: The user says "It is only Safari that does it. Chrome says somewhere between 34ms and 70ms". They may want an explanation and possibly a fix. We should present the plan and ask whether they want the optimization or to disable SW on Safari. Since plan mode, no edits.

If Chrome returns empty too, Chrome also calls `clients.matchAll`, but it's fast. The code comment may be outdated. The key is Safari's `matchAll`/Cache API/SW startup is slower. We can mention that the code's assumption is browser-specific and Safari hits the fallback.

Let's check `sw.js` line numbers and code for the plan. We have them.

Let's also consider the `cache: "reload"` in Safari: Safari may ignore `cache: "reload"` or handle it differently; it may force a network fetch. The server response is fast. Not 500ms.

Let's think about the in-memory known-clients fast path and correctness:
- The page posts its wid after boot with `event.source.id`. In Safari, `event.source` is a `Client` with an id. The worker can store it.
- On a navigation with empty `clientId`, if `known.size === 1`, use that wid. But if the user has one tab and opens a second tab, the first tab's known entry remains; the second tab's page posts its wid, so known.size becomes 2. Until the second tab's page loads, a navigation in the second tab has no known client (the second tab hasn't posted yet). The first tab's entry is the only one, so the worker would wrongly use the first tab's wid for the second tab's first navigation. This is a correctness bug: two tabs could share state. The current code deliberately fails open when ambiguous. So the single-known-client fast path is unsafe when a new tab is opening. ## Investigation: later browser sessions

The later-session case is harder because the SW registration is **persistent**. Even though the new tab has no `wid` yet, the browser still dispatches its first navigation to the installed SW. The SW must boot before it can decide “no wid → fail open”, so you pay the cold-start cost even though the SW does no useful work.

The SW cannot know “this tab has no wid” without booting, and the browser cannot know “this navigation doesn’t need the SW” from the URL.

### Options investigated

**1. Navigation preload — not sufficient**

Navigation preload starts the network request in parallel with SW boot. But the browser still waits for the SW to run the fetch handler before it can use the response. With a 3 ms network and a ~500 ms boot, the perceived delay remains roughly the boot time. It helps when the network is slow, not when the worker is cold.

**2. Keepalive — only helps while a tab is open**

A periodic page → SW message keeps the worker warm. This fixes reloads within an open tab, but not the first navigation after the browser/tab has been closed.

**3. Unregister the SW when the last tab closes — handles later sessions**

This is the only web-platform way to make the next session’s first navigation uncontrolled and fast.

Flow:

1. Last tab closes.
2. Page sends `{ type: "pathland-pagehide" }` to the SW.
3. SW waits a short grace period, then checks `self.clients.matchAll({ type: "window", includeUncontrolled: true })`.
4. If no other windows remain, `self.registration.unregister()`.
5. Next session’s first navigation has no SW registration → goes straight to the network.
6. The page loads, registers the SW in the background, stores the new `wid`, and starts the keepalive.
7. Reload now has a `wid`; the SW is warm and attaches it immediately.

Sketch:

```js
async function unregisterIfLastClient(senderId) {
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 2000));
  const windows = await self.clients.matchAll({
    type: "window",
    includeUncontrolled: true,
  });
  const others = windows.filter((client) => client.id !== senderId);
  if (others.length === 0) {
    await self.registration.unregister();
  }
}
```

Page side:

```ts
window.addEventListener("pagehide", (event) => {
  if ((event as PageTransitionEvent).persisted) return; // bfcache
  stopKeepalive();
  (navigator.serviceWorker.controller ?? reg.active)?.postMessage({
    type: "pathland-pagehide",
  });
}, { once: true });
```

The 2-second grace period handles reloads and navigations: the next document becomes a window client, so the SW does not unregister. If the tab is really closing, no other client appears and the SW removes itself.

**4. Disable the SW and rely on WebSocket resync**

Guaranteed fast first navigation in all sessions, but the SSR renders defaults and the live connection corrects state. This loses the first-paint state scoping the SW was added for.

**5. Other state transports**

A per-tab `wid` in a cookie is not per-tab (cookies are shared). A `wid` in the URL would leak into the address bar/history. A custom navigation header is not settable by page JS. So there is no clean alternative that preserves per-tab first-paint scoping without the SW.

## Reliability caveats

- **Browser crash / force quit**: the pagehide message may never be processed, so the registration can persist. The next session’s first navigation may still be cold. No web API can guarantee cleanup at browser shutdown.
- **Grace-period race**: if a reload/navigation takes longer than 2 s to create the next window client, the SW may unregister early. The page re-registers on load, so this is recoverable but may cause one uncontrolled navigation.
- **Hidden/background tabs**: timers may be throttled; the `visibilitychange`/`focus` ping helps, but a reload immediately after returning may race the warm-up.
- **Resource cost**: the keepalive keeps a worker thread alive while a tab is open.

By “clean tab close” I mean the browser actually delivers the page’s `pagehide` event and keeps the service worker alive long enough to run the 2-second grace timer:

- closing the last tab while the browser stays running,
- navigating away to another site.

It is **not** reliable when:

- the browser is force-quit or crashes,
- the OS kills the process,
- the machine loses power,
- the whole browser quits immediately after the last tab closes, before the SW’s 2 s timer completes.

In those cases the registration can persist, and the next session’s first navigation may still pay a cold start. You said that is acceptable.

So the guarantee is: **normal tab/window close → next session’s first navigation is uncontrolled and fast.** Full browser quit is best-effort.

### 4. Should we clear the `pathland-sw` cache when unregistering?

**Yes — but only when we actually unregister because no other windows remain.**

Why:

- The cache holds `clientId → wid` mappings. Client ids are per-document/session and are never reused after those documents are gone.
- A new tab generates a new `wid`; old entries are dead weight.
- Without cleanup, the cache grows with every tab/session.
- It is safe only when no other window is open; other tabs may still need their mappings.
- Do not clear it on reload/navigation or when another tab remains.

So the unregister path should be:

```js
if (others.length === 0) {
  await caches.delete("pathland-sw");
  await self.registration.unregister();
}
```

## Final plan

### Page side (`lib/typescript/src/service-worker.ts`)

- After `navigator.serviceWorker.ready`, start a **20 s** keepalive interval posting `{ type: "pathland-keepalive" }` to `controller ?? reg.active`.
- Ping on `visibilitychange` → visible and on `focus`.
- On non-bfcache `pagehide`:
  - clear the keepalive interval,
  - post `{ type: "pathland-pagehide" }`.
- On bfcache `pageshow` (`event.persisted`):
  - re-post the `wid`,
  - restart the keepalive.
- Keep the existing `wid` seeding on `ready`, `controllerchange`, and `updatefound`.

### Worker side (`lib/typescript/sw.js`)

- Ignore `pathland-keepalive`.
- Handle `pathland-pagehide`:
  ```js
  async function unregisterIfLastClient(senderId) {
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 2000));
    const windows = await self.clients.matchAll({
      type: "window",
      includeUncontrolled: true,
    });
    const others = windows.filter((client) => client.id !== senderId);
    if (others.length === 0) {
      await caches.delete("pathland-sw");
      await self.registration.unregister();
    }
  }
  ```
  Call it via `event.waitUntil(...)`.
- Add an in-memory `Map<clientId, wid>`:
  - `remember` writes memory first, then Cache API.
  - `recall` checks memory first, then Cache API.
- In the navigation fetch handler:
  ```js
  const response = await fetch(url.toString(), { ... });
  event.waitUntil(remember(event.resultingClientId, wid));
  return response;
  ```

### Tests

- `sw-script.test.ts`:
  - keepalive does not touch the cache,
  - pagehide with another window does not unregister,
  - pagehide with no other window clears the cache and unregisters after the grace period.
- `service-worker.test.ts`:
  - keepalive interval posts `pathland-keepalive`,
  - non-bfcache `pagehide` clears the timer and posts `pathland-pagehide`,
  - bfcache `pagehide` does not unregister,
  - bfcache `pageshow` re-posts the `wid` and restarts keepalive.

### Build and verify

```bash
cd lib/typescript
npm run typecheck
npm test
npm run build:all
```

Then rebuild the native image and test:

1. Fresh install: first navigation uncontrolled and fast.
2. Reload after >30 s: warm SW, fast.
3. Close the last tab normally, reopen the site: first navigation uncontrolled and fast.
4. Close one of two tabs: SW must stay registered.
5. Reload/navigate within the site: SW must not unregister.
6. bfcache back/forward: SW must not unregister.
7. Force-quit the browser: accept a possible cold start on the next first navigation.

The bfcache test got 6 wid messages, not 2. Why? The `seed` is called multiple times: `post()` immediate, `reg.addEventListener("updatefound", seed)`, `navigator.serviceWorker.ready.then(seed)`, `controllerchange`. The fake `ready` resolves, and maybe the previous test's listeners? Each test creates a new `setupServiceWorker`, but old `window`/`document` listeners from previous tests remain. The old `pageshow` listeners also fire on the bfcache `pageshow` event, each posting wid to the current fake container (because `target()` uses `navigator.serviceWorker.controller` at call time). That explains 6 wid messages (multiple old setups). The test's expectation should be >=2, not exactly 2. Or we should isolate listeners. Simpler: assert that after pageshow, the number of wid messages is greater than before. But the old listeners also fire on the pagehide? The bfcache pagehide old listeners return (persisted true). The pageshow old listeners call `postWid` and `startKeepAlive`, posting to current fake. So the count increases by more than one. Change the assertion to `toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(2)` or compare before/after. Better: capture `const beforeWid = fake.messages.filter(...).length;` then after pageshow expect `length > beforeWid`. But `before` was the total messages length. Let's change to:
```ts
const beforeWid = fake.messages.filter(m => m.type === "pathland-wid").length;
...
await vi.waitFor(() => expect(fake.messages.filter(...).length).toBeGreaterThan(beforeWid));
```
This is robust. Also, the old pageshow listeners from previous tests may cause unexpected messages, but we only care that at least one new wid is posted. Good.

Alternatively, avoid old listener accumulation by using a module-level cleanup; but not necessary. We'll adjust the test.

Also, the test "does not unregister on a bfcache pagehide" asserts `fake.messages.length` unchanged after bfcache pagehide. Old pagehide listeners from previous tests with persisted true return; no messages. But old pagehide listeners from previous tests may have `closing` false and persisted true -> return. Good. However, old keepalive intervals from previous tests? afterEach dispatched pagehide and stopped them. But the old `pageshow` listeners could restart keepalive? They only run on pageshow. The bfcache test dispatches a pageshow after the assertion, which restarts old keepalive intervals too! Those old intervals post keepalive to the current fake, and after the test, afterEach dispatches pagehide; old pagehide listeners (closing false?) For old setups, their `closing` may be false (they were stopped by afterEach pagehide which set closing=true). Wait, afterEach pagehide for each test sets `closing=true` and stops. So old `pageshow` persisted handler sets `closing=false` and `startKeepAlive`, restarting old intervals. Then afterEach pagehide (non-persisted) will set closing=true and stop. Good. The test's `vi.waitFor` may see keepalive messages, but we filter wid. Fine.
- The old `pageshow` handlers also post wid, causing the 6. We'll adjust.

Element — `closest` then threw `t.closest is not a function`. `nodeOf`/
  `eventNodeOf` guard with `instanceof Element` and return `null` for a non-Element
  target (unit-tested in `test/dom-target.test.ts`). Aborted promises are also
  swallowed: a media `play()` interrupted by a src change/pause (`AbortError`) and
  a Blob `arrayBuffer()` aborted on socket close no longer surface as unhandled
  rejections.
- **Per-window-id service worker** (issue #155): when the server emits
  `data-pathland-service-worker` on `<html>`, `boot()` registers `{base}/sw.js` at
  the **root** scope and hands the worker this window's id (`postMessage`, re-seeded
  on `ready`/`controllerchange` — a single post can be missed while `reg.active` is
  still null); the worker (`sw.js`, shipped next to the bundle) attaches the id to
  top-level navigations so the SSR renders the right persisted-state scope on the
  first paint — the id never appears in the URL. Absent → any existing registration
  is removed (the kill switch). Strictly pass-through: it never caches and fails open
  (any error → the original request); the id is keyed per tab in the Cache API under
  an **absolute** key URL (a relative `Request` URL is rejected by WebKit) and carried
  across documents via `resultingClientId`. The rewrite builds an **explicit** fetch
  init — never the navigation `Request`, whose `mode: "navigate"` a script cannot
  construct (passing it made `fetch` throw and fail open silently) — with
  `cache: "reload"` (so a same-window reload is never served a stale SSR body); a
  store/rewrite failure is `console.warn`ed in the worker's console, not swallowed.
  **Engine variance**: Chrome reports the *initiating* document's client id on the
  navigation fetch event, WebKit reports an **empty** `clientId` (only
  `resultingClientId`). The worker therefore resolves the id by `clientId` first, then
  falls back to client identity **only when unambiguous** — the sole window client, or
  the single client whose URL equals the request URL (a reload) — and otherwise fails
  open, so a navigation can never be scoped to another window's state.
- **Service-worker E2E** (`e2e/`, Playwright, Chromium + WebKit, `npm run test:e2e`):
  serves the shipped `sw.js` + a bundle of the real `src/service-worker.ts` from a tiny
  fixture server and asserts the next navigation carries the window id. Real worker
  engines are the only place the variance above is observable — jsdom/happy-dom cannot
  reproduce it, which is how the WebKit bug shipped.
- **SSR-scoped marker + initial-resync skip** (issue #155): the server emits
  `data-pathland-ssr-scoped` on `<html>` when the request carried a `wid`, i.e. the
  document was rendered with this window's persisted state. `shouldInitialResync`
  (`src/transport.ts`) then skips the client's initial `META::RESYNC` — the live
  session shares the scope. A reload whose SSR could **not** be scoped (no `wid`
  reached the server) or a stale `?wid=` the window did not adopt still resyncs.
  Sequence-gap and reconnect recovery are unaffected.
- **Hydration-aware TREE reconciliation** (`src/apply.ts`): `CREATE_NODE` reuses an
  existing hydrated element (id already in the registry) and `INSERT_CHILD` skips
  when the child is already in the parent's container — so a resync'd full
  snapshot reconciles against the SSR DOM without clobbering or duplicating.
- **Runtime shells mirror the Rust renderer** (`src/elements.ts`): runtime-created
  nodes carry the same `pathland-*` classes/structure as SSR (a reinstated
  `BUTTON` gets `pathland-button`, `GAUGE` gets its `pathland-gauge` bar shell);

input.newString:
**Engine variance**: Chrome reports the *initiating* document's client id on the
  navigation fetch event, WebKit reports an **empty** `clientId` (only
  `resultingClientId`). The worker therefore resolves the id by `clientId` first, then
  falls back to client identity **only when unambiguous** — the sole window client, or
  the single client whose URL equals the request URL (a reload) — and otherwise fails
  open, so a navigation can never be scoped to another window's state.
  **Worker lifetime**: a cold worker delays a controlled navigation by its boot time,
  so the page pings `pathland-keepalive` every 20 s (plus on focus/visibility) to keep
  the worker warm while a tab is open; the worker also keeps a per-lifetime in-memory
  `clientId → wid` map (Cache API fallback) and does not block the navigation response
  on the Cache API write (`event.waitUntil`). On a non-bfcache `pagehide` the page asks
  the worker to `pathland-pagehide`; after a 2 s grace period the worker checks
  `clients.matchAll`, and if no other window remains it clears the `pathland-sw` cache
  and unregisters itself — so the next browser session's first navigation is
  uncontrolled and does not pay a cold start. A reload/in-site navigation keeps the
  worker registered because the next document appears as a window client.
